#3183. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.

#3181. Palantir Stock Investors Just Got Great News From a Wall Street Analyst (Hint: The Stock Could Soar)

JPMorgan Chase analyst Brian Essex believes Palantir is deeply undervalued.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR +3.48%) has been one of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in both share price appreciation and business expansion. The stock has added 2,400% since ChatGPT popularized generative AI in January 2023, and revenue growth has accelerated in 13 consecutive quarters.

Palantir investors recently got great news. In late October, JPMorgan Chase analyst Brian Essex initiated coverage of the company, awarding Palantir a buy rating and a target price of $262 per share. That is one of the most bullish forecasts on Wall Street and it implies 63% upside from the current share price of $160.

Palantir develops analytics platforms that help government and commercial customers integrate and make sense of complex data. The company supplements its core analytics products with an integrated artificial intelligence (AI) platform called AIP, which serves as a large language model orchestration tool that lets clients swap models without rewriting applications, while retaining control over their sensitive data.

Brian Essex at JPMorgan Chase argues that Palantir has a durable economic moat in its ontology-based software. An ontology unifies data from disparate systems into critical workflows, helping clients make better decisions and automate business processes. For example, Palantir can help manufacturers navigate supplier delays by identifying which customer orders are at risk and deciding how to reallocate inventory.

Forrester Research recently recognized Palantir as a leader in AI platforms. In terms of current capabilities, the analysts ranked its platform above products from all competitors except C3.ai, but the report distinguished Palantir as having the stronger growth strategy. "Palantir's strategy is to build and offer a platform that can accommodate the world's most difficult and highest-return AI use cases."

JPMorgan Chase analyst Brian Essex justified his target price in a recent note. "As we move from a year where enterprises are just figuring out how to deploy the most transformational technology we have seen in our lifetime to one where they are looking for return, Palantir is already delivering ROI by leveraging its platform to fundamentally transform the business operations of its customers, and growth is acceleratingcustomers, and growth is accelerating."

Indeed, Palantir has consistently delivered impressive financial results. In the third quarter, revenue increased 96% to $2.3 billion, marking the 13th straight acceleration. That strong top-line growth was driven largely by momentum in the U.S. commercial business, where sales increased 119%. Meanwhile, non-GAAP earnings soared 144% to $0.44 per diluted share.

In his shareholder letter, CEO Alex Karp wrote, "We have now essentially doubled our entire business since the same quarter last year." And he expects that strength to persist for the foreseeable future. Palantir raised its full-year guidance, with sales now forecast to climb 156% to $8.5 billion in 2026, a significant acceleration from the 75% sales growth reported in 2025.

For many investors, Palantir's rich valuation punches a hole in the investment thesis. Yes, the company has emerged as the standard in enterprise AI, and its business is growing at a phenomenal pace. But the current valuation of 53 times sales makes it the most expensive stock in the S&P 500, with Moderna ranking second at 47 times sales.

Is the business growing quickly enough to justify that valuation multiple? Brian Essex at JPMorgan says the answer is yes. "Valuation is reasonable when taking into account the company's uniquely profitable hyper-growth fundamentals, with potential for substantial disruptive upside within its primary market segments," he wrote in a note to clients.

Many Wall Street analysts agree with Essex and think the stock is undervalued at its current price. In fact, among 38 analysts who follow the company, Palantir has a median target price of $235 per share. That implies 46% upside from the current share price of $160.

#3180. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3179. 10 States Where Residents Face the Steepest Risk from Social Security Cuts

If cuts happen as projected, no state will be spared, and cuts will average around $500 per month.

Many people, especially retirees, pay a lot of attention to Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs). That makes sense, because many of those in retirement need every dollar of benefits, and any increase makes life easier. The upcoming increase for 2027 is 3.6%.

There's a much bigger issue for people to focus on, though: a big potential cut in benefits -- which is likely to be bigger in some states than others.

Here's the situation: Social Security works by collecting taxes from workers and using that income to pay retirees. For many decades, this resulted in a surplus, as Social Security collected more than it paid out.

But times have changed. People are living longer, on average, and many are retiring earlier. So Social Security is paying out more than it's collecting, and that's draining the surplus.

You can see how the ratio of workers to Social Security beneficiaries has shrunk over time in the table below:

Ratio of Covered Workers to Beneficiaries

Data source: Social Security Administration. *projected, in the 2026 Social Security Trustees report

If nothing is done to strengthen it, Social Security's trust funds' surplus will run out within a few years, which will result in benefits shrinking to around 78% of the amount due to beneficiaries. That's a hefty 22% cut. The percentage of the expected cut has fluctuated over the years, and by the time it happens -- if it happens -- it might be a bit larger or smaller. In the 2025 report from the Trustees of the Social Security and Medicare trust funds, the expected cut was 24%.

A 22% cut will turn a $2,500 monthly benefit check into a $1,950 one, smaller by $550 -- each month. That's the bad news. The good news is that there are multiple ways to save Social Security, should Congress decide to do so -- and the newly elected Democratic-majority Congress may well take action.

The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) used projections from the 2025 Trustees of the Social Security and Medicare trust funds report and modeled a 24% cut across all 50 states. It found that the largest cuts would affect retirees in the following 10 states:

Average retiree's cut in monthly benefits

Data source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

Those average cuts vary because average benefit checks vary by state, with retirees in some states having lower incomes than those in other states. So while a smaller expected cut might seem good, it's only because the benefit was smaller to begin with.

The CRFB ended its report saying: "With insolvency projected to occur during the terms of the next elected Senators and President, candidates and policymakers must decide how they will secure a program vital to millions of Americans. That starts with putting forward a plan because if Social Security becomes insolvent – no state would be spared."

This may be quite alarming to you, but keep in mind that for many retirees, Social Security benefits will only provide some retirement income. Most of us should be saving and investing to build a nest egg that can help support us in the future, along with Social Security benefits. After all, the average monthly Social Security retirement benefit was only $2,089 as of September, amounting to around $25,000 annually.

So be sure to come up with a solid retirement plan, detailing how much income you'll need and how you'll achieve it. You may need to save and invest a lot more. You may want to delay retiring for a few years, too.

It can also help to let your representatives in Washington, D.C. know that you don't want to see any Social Security cuts.

#3178. If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation

Merlin Bise is the CTO of Inbenta. He has built conversational AI since before generative AI.

​A lot of the AI deployed into the customer experience over the past three years isn’t performing. That’s just the reality. And the default response I hear, over and over, is to start all over again, evaluating and paying for a new platform.

In most cases, that’s an expensive way to rebuild the same problem.

I’ve been building AI for customer experience since before generative AI showed up. I watched intent matching give way to generative layers, and now we’re into agentic systems that can reason and act on their own. The platforms keep changing. But it isn’t the model that causes the deployment to fail—it’s the knowledge underneath it. I’ve seen that pattern in nearly every underperforming deployment I’ve looked at, going back years.

And look, none of this is a knock on the decision you made three years ago. You made it with the tools that existed then. Those were very different tools.

Here’s what’s new. Fixing the knowledge layer used to be a multiyear, hand-built project. That’s why re-platforming seemed faster, even when it wasn’t. AI now does the heavy lifting up front. It reads, structures and tags your content before anything goes live, so what customers hear is approved, not improvised. Work that used to take a room full of contractors a full year can now get done in weeks, not quarters. If you wrote off your knowledge problem 12 or 18 months ago as too slow or too expensive, it deserves a second look and, honestly, a lot more optimism than it would have earned back then.

Before you run another evaluation, check three things. You can diagnose all of them without a new vendor.

Content written for someone browsing a help site does a different job than content a model has to parse. A model can have the right document and still give the wrong answer. Why? Because two records that aren’t the same can look the same to a system reading them. If a customer asks about one product configuration and gets information about another, that isn’t because the company chose the wrong model or the customer botched the prompt. It’s a structure and authorship problem, and no new platform is going to fix it for you.

Count them. Most organizations have more duplication than they think. As mentioned earlier, a lot of platforms started with intent matching, then added a generative layer later and kept the original intent base underneath. So, now you’ve got two copies of your content, two governance surfaces and two possible answers to the same question. Contact center stacks do the same thing by channel—one store for digital and another for voice. The answer changes depending on which door the customer walked through. If a policy lives in more than one place, you have a consistency problem, not an AI problem.

This is the one that kills deployments. If the subject matter expert who spots a wrong answer has to file a ticket and wait on an engineer, corrections will never keep pace with the business. The person with the knowledge can’t act. The person who can act has no way to judge whether the answer was right. Give that six months, and the system has drifted away from how the company is supposed to operate, without a single error in the logs. You don’t get an alert—you get confused customers.

In the end, you should have one knowledge store instead of several, content structured so a machine can find the right answer and the people who own the policies in control of the answers. And there’s no need to replace your platform.

The economics back this approach up. A full platform replacement is a six-figure commitment before you even count internal time, and moving off an entrenched stack can run several times that. Fixing the knowledge layer costs a fraction of it. And you keep the asset, no matter what you run on top. If you want to switch platforms later, fine. You’ll be moving a structured, governed knowledge base, instead of hauling the same mess to a new vendor and paying them to discover it.

There’s a second-order benefit, too. A consolidated, governed knowledge layer gives you an audit trail. When a regulator asks about a specific conversation, you need to show the question, the answer, the source and who approved it. It doesn’t matter what platform was used. If you can’t see why your AI said something, you can’t defend it.

Here’s my takeaway. Before you run another evaluation, figure out whether you have a platform problem or a foundation problem. Most of the time, it’s the foundation. And it’s more fixable today than it was when you signed that original contract.

Each year, the IRS adjusts tax brackets to keep pace with inflation. The 2027 tax brackets were announced on Nov. 5, 2026.

The IRS has released updated tax brackets for 2027, which apply to the taxes we file in 2028. You may notice that the seven tax rates generally stay the same year-to-year — so why do tax brackets get adjusted?

Well, due to inflation, our money might not stretch as far as it did the previous year. To combat that, the IRS adjusts tax brackets so taxpayers can keep a little bit more of their money in a lower tax bracket compared with the previous year.

For example, a single filer could make up to $50,400 in 2026 and pay a top tax rate of 12%. But in 2027, they could make up to $52,025 and still only pay a top tax rate of 12% thanks to these inflation adjustments.

Not sure how to read the tax bracket tables below?

Find your total taxable income in the "tax bracket" column. The corresponding tax rate is the highest rate you'll pay — it doesn’t apply to all your income; it applies only to the portion that falls within that bracket. The income in the lower brackets is taxed at those lower rates.

For example, let's say you’re a single filer and you expect to earn $150,000 this year. The top rate you’d pay on a portion of your income is 24%. The rest would be taxed at 10%, 12% and 22%.

#3176. These 4 Stocks Are Tied to the Smartphone in Your Pocket

Which of these four businesses is still earning more money from your phone?

Apple (AAPL -0.52%), Qualcomm (QCOM +5.53%), Corning (GLW +2.61%), and Arm Holdings (ARM +4.74%) each collect a share of the money spent on smartphones. Apple sells the phone. Qualcomm supplies chips and patent licenses, Corning makes the glass over the screen, and Arm's chip designs turn up in almost all smartphones.

But their latest quarterly reports all vary meaningfully. Apple's iPhone revenue climbed 17% year over year in the September quarter, while Qualcomm's handset chip revenue dropped 26%. And Corning and Arm both said a softer smartphone market hurt their results.

All four also pointed to the same pressure: memory chips have become much pricier. But I think it matters really differently for each stock.

Apple makes much more money from the phone than the other three do. iPhone sales were around $254 billion for fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 26. That was 53% of Apple's revenue and 21% more than a year earlier.

But growth is slowing. iPhone revenue climbed 17% year over year to $57.6 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, after gaining around 22% in fiscal Q3. And excluding the benefit of tariff refunds, Apple's gross margin dipped about one point from the June quarter. Management sees it coming in between 45% and 46% in the holiday quarter, mainly because of memory costs.

At roughly $347 as of this writing, Apple trades at about 36 times its expected fiscal 2027 earnings. Investors are paying a premium as its margins fall.

Qualcomm's phone business is going the other way. Its handset chip revenue dropped 26% year over year to around $5.1 billion in its fiscal fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 27. It had risen 3% in fiscal Q1, then dropped 13% in Q2 and 20% in Q3. For the full fiscal year, Qualcomm blamed lower shipments to some major phone makers, which cut their build plans as memory got scarcer and pricier.

And Qualcomm expects Apple to rely mostly on its own modems from now on, a change it warns will significantly hit its chip sales.

Of course, Qualcomm still collects from the phone through its patents. It renewed its long-term license with Apple, and licensing kept 70% of its revenue as pre-tax profit in the quarter, versus 24% for the chip business. Meanwhile, auto chip revenue surged 89% to nearly $2 billion.

At roughly $150, Qualcomm trades at about 15 times the earnings it's expected to report in fiscal 2027. I'd say the price already assumes the handset business keeps shrinking.

Corning's links with Apple stretch back almost 20 years.

"By the end of 2026, all the cover glass for iPhone, including iPhone Duo, and Apple Watch, sold worldwide will be produced at our Harrodsburg, Kentucky facility," chief financial officer Ed Schlesinger said on Corning's Oct. 27 earnings call.

Phone glass, though, is in Corning's glass innovations segment, which also sells glass for TVs and laptops. Segment sales slipped 3% in the third quarter, to about $1.5 billion, and segment net income slid 10%.

Optical communications, meanwhile, grew sales 44% to around $2.4 billion, and Corning's sales linked to generative AI more than doubled. With shares near $104, Corning trades at about 23 times next year's expected earnings, a price I think largely depends on fiber.

About 43% of Arm's royalties in the fiscal year ended March 31 came from the main smartphone processors.

In the September quarter, royalty revenue dropped to $670 million, down from $715 million three months earlier, and grew just 8% year over year. Arm said memory prices hit the smartphone market, partly offsetting a doubling in data center royalties.

Around $166 as of this writing, Arm stock trades at about 55 times expected earnings for fiscal 2028, which for Arm ends in March 2028. Investors are probably paying that premium for the data center, where Arm expects Arm-based chips to make up more than 60% of the server market at the largest cloud providers by the end of 2026.

Ultimately, of the four, only Apple reported growing phone sales last quarter.

Sure, about 36 times expected earnings isn't cheap, and memory costs might pressure Apple's margins for a while. But Apple sets the device's price, and it raised iPhone prices in September. Qualcomm is much cheaper, but its handset revenue is still falling.

For the phone itself, I'd consider buying Apple.

#3175. ​The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure

Bill Wong - AI Research Fellow, Info-Tech Research Group.

​​In my previous article, we examined the emergence of a new data center asset, the AI factory, which is optimized to run AI workloads. Compared to traditional data centers, AI data center campuses require up to 10 times the total facility power capacity, driven by GPU server racks that consume 12 to 28 times more power per rack and thermal density that requires advanced liquid cooling to handle five times the heat generation.

This new industrial revolution is driving an unprecedented demand for power, transforming the utilities industry from a relatively stable and quiet industry to a growth sector.​ Nations and organizations alike will need to optimize their AI energy strategy in order to flourish during and after this revolution.

After reviewing several national AI energy infrastructure strategies around the world, four distinct strategies stand out. These strategies will shape how nations are planning to build the required energy infrastructure for AI workloads.

• Sovereign Regulation-Driven: These jurisdictions introduce legislation to ensure that AI developers must fund their own power requirements, maintain the reliability of the grid and provide the supporting water infrastructure required for these data centers to prevent rising utility costs. In Canada, the country’s recently published AI strategy champions their grid’s 83% investment in clean power. Australia will require data center providers to generate as much energy as they consume. The EU has introduced a sovereign AI compute platform, EuroHPC JU, which aims to “develop innovative energy-efficient HPC software technologies tailored to exascale and post-exascale supercomputers.”

• Market-Driven: These countries rely on the private sector to drive the building of data centers and leverage easily accessible energy resources. The U.S. has begun by reinvesting into nuclear power plants and the use of small modular reactors. The UK has accelerated AI projects through its AI Growth Zones, fast track permits.

• Localization-Driven: Rather than adding additional workloads to the existing energy grids, some countries are locating new data centers near clean energy sources. Japan’s new collaboration strategy leverages nine designated green energy zones. South Korea’s new strategy directs the movement of 18.4 GW of data center workloads out of Seoul to regional nuclear and small modular reactor clusters.

• State-Driven: China’s government is planning to connect renewable energy resources from its western region to its computing hubs in its eastern region.​

In order to assess a nation or organization’s AI energy strategy, one must examine its energy value chain. This involves identifying the source of its energy, determining how power is generated, determining how power is managed and deployed, understanding the nation’s thermal management and understanding the sustainability strategy the nation or organization has implemented.​

Meaningful metrics in this area focus on the total volume, dependability and carbon footprint of the electricity required by the organization in question’s compute infrastructure. Countries and organizations using clean and renewable energy resources will be able to differentiate their energy infrastructure in a positive manner. On the other hand, countries leveraging fossil fuels, like natural gas, may have the short-term benefit of accessing low-cost energy resources, but they will also encounter long-term emissions problems, which expose them to carbon regulation and creates cost volatility.​

Metrics in this area focus on an energy infrastructure’s capacity and its ability to connect, control and optimize high-density energy flow between the bulk electric grid (external) and its computing facilities (internal).

From a macro-grid point of view, which focuses outside of the data center, leaders can use ultra-high-voltage transmission lines, battery storage and AI-driven load-balancing software to absorb the violent swings in demand from GPU clusters, which can dramatically improve power management.

From a micro-grid standpoint, which focuses inside the data center, leaders have a few things to consider. Today’s AI racks demand 130 to 600 kW, and pushing that much power through legacy wiring can generate wasted heat and requires multiple inefficient conversion steps. Modern operators can implement ±400V or 800V DC systems and solid-state transformers to reduce internal heat loss and conversion steps.​

Legacy air cooling can no longer dissipate the heat generated by today’s AI factories. How a company handles this heat is becoming a competitive advantage for any organization running its own sovereign AI infrastructure. I’ve observed some leading operators switching to direct-to-chip liquid cooling in closed-loop systems, which can slash operational water consumption.

Embracing robust environmental stewardship can help nations and organizations keep their data center expansion efforts sustainable, minimizing ecological disruption while preserving critical local environmental resources. Beyond conservation, some advanced operators are turning thermal management into a revenue stream. By establishing facilities in colder climates (like Canada, the Nordics or Hokkaido, Japan) and capturing the 60- to 80-degree Celsius waste heat directly from server racks, those operators can sell that heat to municipal district heating networks.​

Which AI energy infrastructure strategy is the best for a given organization will depend on several factors, and not all options are available for a given country or geographical location, especially those strategies that can leverage a country’s colder climate to reduce cooling costs.

Countries and organizations need to prioritize and align their energy infrastructure architecture with their nation’s sovereign AI strategy. For instance, sustainability initiatives will likely have the best success in countries like Canada and Nordic nations.

Finally, organizations need to learn how to address the current backlash from people regarding AI data centers near their communities. Builders and operators should be prepared to address questions and concerns surrounding the AI energy value chain they’re leveraging, along with its regional costs and benefits. Leaders should focus on sustainability, environmental impact and delivering an accountability framework for the operations of their proposed AI data center.​

#3173. A $120 Billion Westinghouse Reactor Plan Is Taking Shape. Here’s What History Says Happened the Last Time the U.S. Built Them.

The last AP1000 builds in the U.S. blew past their budgets and bankrupted Westinghouse. This time the structure looks different, and that’s what matters.

The U.S. government recently signed a new framework agreement with South Korea to support the deployment of Westinghouse technology in the U.S. The new framework commits up to $120 billion of investment by South Korea to help finance the construction of eight large reactors on federal sites, six Westinghouse AP1000s and two Korean APR1400 reactors that incorporate Westinghouse technology.

For investors in Brookfield Renewable (BEPC +1.50%)(BEP +1.63%) and Cameco (CCJ +4.35%), which currently co-own Westinghouse, that's a very exciting development. However, before you get too excited, you'll want to see what history says about the last time Westinghouse built AP1000s in the U.S. Here's a look back at the last build cycle and why the setup looks different this time.

In 2008, Westinghouse signed fixed-price contracts to build two AP1000 nuclear reactors at Plant Vogtle in Georgia and two more at V.C. Summer in South Carolina. The company initially expected Vogtle to cost $14 billion and V.C. Summer to cost $9.8 billion. However, due to delays and other factors, costs ballooned out of control, causing Westinghouse to file for bankruptcy in 2017. The utilities developing V.C. Summer abandoned the project in 2017 after the cost estimate soared to $25 billion, even after already investing $9 billion. Meanwhile, Southern Company took over construction management at Vogtle and eventually finished Unit 3 in 2023 and Unit 4 in 2024, spending over $30 billion, more than double the original estimate.

As the old saying goes, this time it's different. Two things stand out. One major difference is the funding strategy. Last time, utilities contracted with Westinghouse to build additional reactors at existing sites they operated, with the utilities funding up to the fixed cost they agreed to with Westinghouse. When it went bankrupt, they were on the hook for 100% of the cost. This time, the U.S. government is deploying the reactors at federal sites, with funding from South Korea. So, instead of utility-led projects, these are government-led projects.

The second difference is Westinghouse's role. According to Brookfield Renewable's latest earnings release, Westinghouse will provide design, engineering, and procurement for the AP1000s, plus long-term maintenance and fuel services. For the two Korean-designed reactors built on Westinghouse technology, Brookfield said Westinghouse would receive upfront licensing fees and a significant scope of work during construction and operations. Westinghouse expects about $2 billion per reactor from intellectual property licensing, engineering and procurement services, subcontracting opportunities and long-term fuel fabrication services. In other words, these aren't fixed-price contracts where it bears any cost overruns.

Brookfield Renewable and its institutional partners own 51% of Westinghouse (Brookfield's actual stake is currently closer to 11%), with Cameco holding 49%. However, those interests will likely get diluted. The framework with South Korea provides for a cornerstone equity investment between 5% and 10% in Westinghouse to align all parties around the long-term growth of its technology. Meanwhile, the U.S. Government can take an equity stake in Westinghouse, depending on its IPO valuation and timing.

That makes Westinghouse a meaningful investment for Cameco and a smaller piece of Brookfield's cash flows. For example, Brookfield's distributed energy, storage, and sustainable solutions segment (which includes its Westinghouse investment) contributed $54 million in funds from operations during the third quarter (16% of the total). However, it highlighted Westinghouse as a bright spot, noting that its operating plants business was up over 20% due in part to progress on new AP1000 reactor developments.

Meanwhile, Cameco reported that its share of Westinghouse's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) was $143 million in the third quarter (54% of its adjusted EBITDA). That was up from $124 million in the year-ago period. Cameco's larger stake makes Westinghouse a more meaningful contributor to its financial results.

Westinghouse is a different company than it was when the U.S. last built AP1000s. However, there's still lots of risk this time around. The South Korean investment is non-binding and subject to final negotiations. The deal may fall apart or end up at a much lower figure than $120 billion and fewer than eight new reactors. Meanwhile, delays and cost overruns could again impact returns. As we saw last time, nuclear reactors are challenging to build.

Brookfield Renewable and Cameco investors should keep an eye on a few things. Whether the U.S. signs definitive agreements with South Korea, who signs the construction contracts and carries the cost risk, and whether Westinghouse will directly participate in the investment build-out. If the contract structure limits Westinghouse's risks, the risk of history repeating would diminish.

Matt DiLallo has positions in Brookfield Renewable and Brookfield Renewable Partners. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Cameco. The Motley Fool recommends Brookfield Renewable and Brookfield Renewable Partners. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Here's a rundown of changes to some well-known tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

Each year, the IRS updates common tax provisions, such as income tax brackets and the standard deduction, to ensure the tax code is keeping pace with the rising cost of living.

These tweaks — formally known as inflation adjustments — help prevent “bracket creep,” where taxpayers who received a cost-of-living raise can pay more in taxes even though their purchasing power remains unchanged.

Inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year were set at 3.2% — larger than the previous two years as inflation heated up. This could mean lower tax bills for some people when they file in 2028.

In the U.S., there are seven marginal rates — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37% — which will remain unchanged for 2027.

Contrary to a popular myth, it’s uncommon for people to pay a single flat federal tax rate on their taxable income. Instead, portions of a person’s income can be taxed at different rates depending on which tax brackets they fall into. For example, some of a person’s income could be taxed at 10%, another chunk at 12%, and so on.

For 2027, the IRS is adjusting those tax brackets — the windows of income that dictate where a tax rate ends and begins — for each filing status. The adjustments mean that some people may be able to keep some of their income in lower tax brackets, and those who received a cost-of-living raise may avoid getting a portion of their income pushed into a higher bracket.

Married filers, for example, can make up to $104,050 to remain with a top tax rate of 12%, compared with $100,800 in 2026. This increase could allow some couples to shelter an additional $3,250 from a higher tax rate in 2027.

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Single filers

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Heads of household

2026 vs. 2027 tax brackets: Married filing separately

» MORE: See the full 2027 tax brackets for each filing status

The IRS lets most filers lower their taxable income by taking the standard deduction or itemizing their returns. The standard deduction, a flat amount based on filing status and age, is popular, as it requires less work to claim and is often more beneficial for those who might not have deductible expenses.

For 2027, the standard deduction will be $16,600 for single filers and those married filing separately, a $500 increase from 2026. Joint filers will be eligible to take $33,200 and heads of household can take $24,925, a $1,000 and $775 increase over 2026, respectively.

» Need help deciding whether to itemize or take the standard deduction? Learn about the differences

Also included in the IRS' 32-page inflation release are various updates to several tax provisions beyond the federal tax brackets. Plus, a brand-new tax credit will go into effect in 2027.

Starting in 2027, taxpayers who contribute to a health flexible spending account (FSA) can contribute up to $3,500 and, if their plan permits, carry over up to $700 into the next tax year.

For those with health savings accounts, the 2027 limit for contributions will rise to $4,500 for self-only coverage and $9,000 for family coverage.

The annual exclusion for gifts, which limits how much taxpayers can give an individual without filing a gift tax return on certain gifts, will be $20,000 per person in 2027, an increase of $1,000 compared with 2026.

The lifetime estate tax exclusion establishes a threshold for the taxation of estates upon a person's death. In 2027, estates valued at or below $15.48 million will not be subject to estate tax, up from $15 million in 2026.

The Education Freedom Tax Credit will launch on Jan. 1. According to the IRS, it aims to support private contributions for K-12 scholarships. Taxpayers who donate to a "scholarship granting organization" in one of the 30 participating states can receive a nonrefundable tax credit of up to $1,700 ($3,400 for couples filing jointly).

#3169. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3166. Prediction: SpaceX Will Not Cancel the Falcon 9 in 2028

Elon Musk has 22.2 billion reasons to rethink retiring Falcon 9 between now and 2028.

16 years after its first flight, the Falcon 9 reusable rocket, workhorse of Space Exploration Technologies' (SPCX +8.62%) space fleet, is getting ready to retire -- or so says Space.com.

With nearly 700 launches (and more than 650 landings) under its belt, the Falcon 9 is the world's second-most-flown rocket ever (after Russia's Soyuz), and the rocket that flies most frequently today. Its payload to orbit (22.8 metric tons) and low launch cost ($74 million) make it arguably one of the most economical means of getting to orbit, too, with a price per kilogram to low earth orbit of only $3,245.

But despite its pedigree, and despite its economics, Space.com calls Falcon's retirement "inevitable" now that Elon Musk has vowed to shift his focus to SpaceX's newer, bigger, better, and cheaper rocket, Starship.

@CJHandmer @SciGuySpace @SpaceX Once Starship is flying reliably several times per week, it makes sense to shift super scarce SpaceX engineering and production resources to Starship to get launch rate to several times per day, which means winding down Falcon

"Beginning in 2028," warns Space.com, "SpaceX may discontinue all but a few Falcon 9 missions" for NASA -- mostly resupply and astronaut transfer missions to the International Space Station -- and switch commercial operations to Starship. Worse news for other space companies: Most of those flights will carry SpaceX's own cargo to orbit as it continues to build out its Starlink internet constellation and seeks to begin deploying artificial intelligence (AI) data centers to low earth orbit.

Considering that Starship launches may cost as little as $10 million each, a fraction of a Falcon 9 launch, that makes good economic sense for SpaceX.

For everyone else, though, it could be a disaster.

In a column last week for tech website Ars Technica, Eric Berger argued that when Falcon 9 withdraws from the commercial market, it will leave a yawning gap in launch supply behind it. "Between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies," warns Berger. Add demand for national security launches servicing the U.S. Space Force, the National Reconnaissance Office, and other security forces, and the rocket gap widens.

And things will get worse before they get better. While multiple small new space companies are trying to build rockets comparable to SpaceX's Falcon, the companies that already possess such rockets -- including United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, and Europe's Arianespace -- have largely found their fleets grounded by a variety of technical glitches. For most space customers who need a ride to space, it's currently SpaceX or bust.

Now, in space, problems are to be expected, but it's reasonable to expect that they will eventually be solved. ULA's Vulcan, Blue Origin's New Glenn, and Ariane's Ariane 6 should all eventually return to flight. None of them are likely to fly anywhere near as frequently as SpaceX's reusable Falcon 9, however. With Falcon leaving the lineup in 2028, Ars Technica's Berger thinks that year will be particularly supply-constrained, and some deficit in space launch capability may last until "late in the 2030s."

Once upon a time, Elon Musk declared: "Imagine you had $6 million in cash on a pallet flying through the air that's just going to smash into the ocean. Would you try to recover that? Yes, you would." And so he built giant fishnets, loaded them on boats, and tried to figure out a way to catch his rocket fairings as they fell back to earth so he could reuse them.

Now consider: Ars Technica's Berger is suggesting there's an untapped market for perhaps 300 rocket launches from now through 2030, worth perhaps $22.2 billion at the most recent advertised launch cost for Falcon 9. No one else can launch these payloads, but SpaceX could if it wanted to. Is Elon Musk -- the man who scrambled to find a way to save just $6 million -- really going to let $22.2 billion "smash into the ocean" without attempting to catch it?

Admittedly, it remains to be seen exactly what Musk will do. Perhaps he'll tweak the design of his Starship rocket (currently optimized for disbursing flat Starlink satellites like a Pez dispenser) so some of them can carry other companies' payloads while others carry Starlink and AI data center satellites exclusively. But I think it's just as likely that once Musk is convinced there's an untapped market for Falcon that's worth multiple billions of dollars -- all his for the taking -- he'll relent on retiring Falcon 9 and permit that rocket to keep flying alongside Starship.

Don't count Falcon 9 out just yet. So long as a market exists, SpaceX will find a way to service it.

#3165. ​Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows

Corey Ercanbrack is CTO at Vasion, leading the AI-native transformation of a cloud-native platform under FedRAMP High.

A state agency mails benefits notices to citizens, with personal data on the page and legal rights tied to what’s printed. When I asked the administrator responsible for its 30,000 endpoints what governs that output process, he said it runs elsewhere, on infrastructure owned by a different team.​

He wasn’t dodging me. That’s how these environments get built, and it produces a blind spot most leaders inherit rather than create. Information is governed where the data lives. Output is governed where the devices live. Those are two teams with different budgets, reporting lines and definitions of accountability, so the artifact carrying the heaviest legal obligation sits furthest from the controls protecting the information inside it.​

The same split appears across other organizations I work with. Major American cities operating under state public records law must produce any official communication upon request, whatever the medium. Their digital channels are instrumented. Paper isn’t. The specialist responsible for its endpoint estate acknowledged that if he sent a printed memo, someone would still have to find it.​

That gap has been survivable because a person stands in it. The employee who printed the memo knows he printed it, and if a request arrives two years later, someone can ask him. In audit terms, he’s a compensating control: what you document and test when the designed control can’t be implemented. Nobody documented this one. It’s been load-bearing for 30 years without appearing in a control matrix, which is why removing it looks costless.​

Agents remove it. Deloitte’s 2026 “State of AI in the Enterprise” report surveyed 3,235 business and IT leaders across 24 countries. Nearly three in four companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, while one in five reports a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Among the capabilities Deloitte names as crucial are audit trails capturing the full chain of agent actions.​

When an instruction comes from a system rather than a person, there may be no human intent to reconstruct later and no awareness that a records obligation was triggered. Unless the workflow was designed to capture that context, automation can generate unaccounted output far faster than the informal human process it replaced. Leaders may be automating away a control they never knew they depended on.

Most AI governance programs are scoped to the application: which model acted, what data it reached, what it was authorized to do and what it produced. That work is necessary, but it is not sufficient, because operational documents don’t stay inside one application.​

I have watched a prior authorization request move from a medical record to paper, to a fax machine, to an insurer and return days later as an email. Each system recorded its portion and completed the step it was designed to handle, but none held the thread connecting them: the only view from which the organization could reconstruct the full event. The application finished its task. The business did not, and governance was scoped to the first while the obligation attaches to the second.​

An IT leader at a global distributor gave me a paperless example. More countries where his company operates now require documents to be deposited with a government authority. The regulation specifies where the document must be sent without specifying how it gets there. Treating the output boundary as a printing problem misses the broader obligation to govern the document throughout its journey.​

If an auditor picked up an AI-generated document tomorrow, what could you prove about it? Four questions help determine the answer.

1. Identity: Who or what produced it? Once a document is printed, exported or faxed, the chain of identity breaks. The artifact no longer shows which agent created it, who initiated the action or where the information came from.​

2. Authorization: Who approved its release? Knowing who generated a document is not the same as knowing whether release was authorized. A finished document proves neither.​

3. Audit: What happened between input and output? An agent extracts information, changes content and generates instructions. Record only the finished document, and you can’t show what it did. The record has to replay what went in, what changed, who acted and where it went.​

4. Retention: Can you find and classify it? Without the first three, you accumulate documents you’re obligated to protect and unable to trace, turning a governance gap into a storage liability.​

Miss one, and you don’t have end-to-end AI governance. Instead, you have a partial record of an action that continued without you. I recommend running these four against a live workflow before expanding agent authority. The gaps you find are the ones an agent will only widen.

The instinct is to connect every system, but these integrations are often fragile and require ongoing maintenance whenever one side changes.

Start with the work instead.​ Pick one operational document this week and follow it from creation to final disposition. Mark every point where somebody prints, exports, faxes, signs, scans or retypes information, and keep going after the data leaves the application. The handoffs are where governance stops without announcing it. Test the four questions at each one. Wherever context breaks, you’ve found the real boundary of your program before an auditor does.​

The workflows that hold up often share one trait: The record was designed before the agent was deployed, rather than reconstructed after someone asked for it. That means someone decided where human review belonged and what needed to be recorded at every step, including the agent’s actions. You can’t deploy first and gather the evidence later. The record has to be created when the action occurs, or it may not exist at all. And the destination is rarely as modern as the agent. I’ve watched sophisticated automation end with a fax because that’s what the recipient accepts.​​

Governance has to follow the information through every handoff. The practical perimeter is everywhere the information goes.​​

#3163. Stock Market Faces a Worst-Case Scenario After Midterm Elections. History Says This Will Happen Next.

The stock market tends to perform poorly when a Republican president serves alongside a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Midterm elections have historically been difficult for the political party in the White House, and this year was no different. Democrats won control of both chambers, flipping at least 42 House seats and seven Senate seats in a sweeping defeat for President Donald Trump's Republican Party.

Wall Street was initially pleased. The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.09%) added 1.6% and 1.4%, respectively, on the day following the election, as investors celebrated the congressional gridlock that will limit Trump's ability to make major policy changes.

However, the indexes gave up those gains and more on Thursday, Nov. 5, due to concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress could bring greater scrutiny to artificial intelligence infrastructure spending. Anxiety surrounding elevated oil prices, persistent inflation, and potential interest rate hikes added to the selling pressure.

Looking ahead, history says a worst-case scenario is about to unfold for the stock market.

The S&P 500 has added 23% since President Trump returned to the White House for a second term in January 2025. That represents an annual return of 12.1%. But statistics suggest the benchmark index will deliver much worse returns throughout the remaining years of Trump's presidency.

There are six possible combinations of presidential party affiliation and congressional control. A Republican president could serve alongside a Republican-controlled Congress, a Democratic-controlled Congress, or a divided Congress. The same three possibilities exist under a Democratic president.

Of those six possibilities, the one produced by the latest midterm elections -- a Republican president paired with a Democratic-controlled Congress -- has historically been the worst combination for the S&P 500. The chart below provides details.

Data source: Carson Investment Research. The chart shows the S&P 500's annual return under different combinations of presidential party affiliation and congressional control. Data was collected between 1951 and 2025.

When a Republican president has served alongside a Democratic-controlled Congress, the S&P 500 has returned 4.9% annually, making it the worst combination for the stock market.

In other words, history says the S&P 500 will add 4.9% annually during the last two years of  Trump's presidency. That equates to a total return of roughly 10%, which falls well short of the 23% return observed during the first two years of his second term.

We can also look at the data from another angle. Excluding the presidential variable, the S&P 500 has generally performed better under a divided Congress, returning an average of 15.1% annually compared with 8.1% annually when either party controls both chambers. Why? Wall Street favors predictability, and a divided Congress is much less likely to make sweeping legislative changes.

Of course, past performance is never a guarantee of future results. The chart above also indicates that the S&P 500 has gained 7.6% annually when a Republican president has served alongside a Republican-controlled Congress. But we have been in that situation for nearly two years and the S&P 500 has added 12.1% annually.

While the combination of a Republican president and a Democratic-controlled Congress has historically been bad news for the stock market, readers should bear in mind that the S&P 500 has still delivered positive returns under those conditions. So, it would not make sense to avoid the stock market solely because the midterm elections shifted the balance of power in Washington.Additionally, the six-month period following midterm elections has historically been the strongest six months of the four-year presidential cycle. During that period, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite have returned an average of 13% and 18%, respectively. And the explanation for those strong returns is simple: With midterm elections in the rearview mirror, there is much less political uncertainty.

#3162. Stop Measuring Technology Adoption And Start Measuring What It Changes

Gayathri Kolandaisami | Doctoral Researcher | Human-centered digital and AI transformation in water utilities and critical infrastructure.

A technology investment can succeed on paper but still fail to solve the problem it was meant to solve.

I saw this happen long before the AI era. When I started my technology career in 2005, my job was to build and maintain the software used by my clients. Over time, I learned that building the technology was only part of the equation. We also needed to understand why it was needed and how the work was being done:

1. What problem were we trying to solve, or what improvement did we want in productivity, efficiency or service delivery?

3. What should the ideal process look like?

That way of thinking stayed with me as my career moved from software development into larger digital transformation projects. It left me with a principle I still believe today: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

I was in a position to observe an organization’s reaction when an AI coding assistant was introduced to its developers. The management had invested in this technology long before I got involved in the organization. However, they hadn’t understood or researched where and how that technology could help the developers, what the benefits of using it would be or whether the tool was apt for their environment. The outcome was a KPI introduced at an organizational level to measure the tool’s adoption. So, a developer was considered to have met this part of their KPI by simply showing that they’d adopted this tool.

This left me asking myself: Had we moved away from measuring the outcomes of the technology to simply measuring its adoption? That’s when I realized that we’d started working for the technology and not the other way around.

Make no mistake—every cell in my body screams technology. I want to develop new technologies that could solve a lot of global challenges. I’m a strong believer in new technologies, and I’m fascinated by how quickly AI is evolving. But I also think that we’re forgetting why we invented these technologies in the first place. Sometimes, we race toward adopting the newest technology without knowing what we were trying to make better.

Technology is a means to solve a problem, improve a process or create a better outcome. The technology itself isn’t the outcome.

I came across a 2025 study published in Management Science. The researchers estimated that using an AI coding assistant increased completed tasks by 26.08%. In contrast, another 2025 study that examined experienced open-source developers working on mature repositories found that developers took 19% longer when using the AI tools that were tested.

The lesson from these studies is that technology doesn’t produce the same result in different environments.​

Organizations can easily measure the wrong outcome.

Take software development, for example. Building new software or making a change to existing software can involve requirements gathering, design, programming, testing, bug fixing and implementation. Let’s say we implemented an AI coding assistant. We may think that this tool could cut programming time substantially. However, that isn’t the whole picture, is it? What happens if the AI-assisted code requires more testing? What if developers spend additional time reviewing and correcting it? What if defects increase, and some of the time saved in programming is consumed later in the process?

If we measure only programming time in this scenario, we may conclude that the technology has been highly successful. However, if we measure the entire journey from requirements to delivery, we may reach a very different conclusion.

The entire process matters when measuring the outcome of the technology. If the problem that the technology is addressing is slow delivery, measure the complete cycle from requirements to release. If the problem is quality, understand defects and rework. If the objective is greater capacity, determine whether the team can actually complete more meaningful work.

The metric should originate from the problem, the context and the process, not simply from the technology.

I prefer piloting the technology before widely adopting it. A pilot isn’t simply an opportunity to prove that a technology works. It’s an opportunity to discover whether it works for your people, your processes and your particular environment.

If employees aren’t using a technology, that should initially be treated as information rather than a performance problem. Perhaps they need training. Perhaps the technology doesn’t fit their workflow. Perhaps it works well for some tasks but not others. Perhaps the existing technology environment, including legacy systems or code, limits its usefulness. Or perhaps it simply isn’t solving a sufficiently important problem.

Adoption is only one part of the story. Technology can also affect employee and customer experience. It may remove repetitive work and allow employees to focus on more meaningful activities, but it may also create additional work when people have to check, correct or validate its output. Some outcomes are tangible, such as time saved, costs reduced, greater capacity or more work completed. Others are harder to quantify, such as employee satisfaction, customer satisfaction, trust and confidence in the service being delivered. They’re still outcomes.

As organizations embrace increasingly powerful technologies, the temptation will be to measure what’s easiest to see: licenses purchased, systems deployed, users onboarded or usage rates. Those numbers have their place, but they don’t answer the most important question: What became better because we introduced the technology?

Always remember: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.
