Basic economy tickets come with plenty of restrictions, but holding the right credit card is my top trick for avoiding some of them.

As airfares remain high, that basic economy fare might look more tempting than ever. Saving $100 on a round-trip domestic flight could mean more money for hotels, dining or other experiences at your destination.

I’ve flown my fair share of basic economy flights, which come with restrictions like being unable to select a seat, earning no award miles and boarding last. You also can’t make changes or cancel your itinerary without paying a hefty fee, and — specific to United Airlines — you can’t bring a full-size carry-on on board.

But as a United frequent flyer, I have a secret to share with you: Holding the United℠ Explorer Card (annual fee: $0 intro for the first year, then $150) lets you avoid several of those basic economy restrictions.

Right now, new United℠ Explorer Card applicants can receive this welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first 3 months your account is open.

Most major airlines no longer let you earn points or miles on basic economy fares. United is an exception, though — assuming you hold the right credit card.

Eligible cardholders, including those who have the United℠ Explorer Card, earn at least 3 miles per $1 spent on United basic economy tickets, excluding taxes and select fees. That’s half of what a standard economy ticket earns for cardholders (6 miles per $1), but it’s better than zero. If you have elite status, you’ll earn more.

Those miles are in addition to the 3 miles per $1 you earn on all United purchases when using your United℠ Explorer Card.

With the card, your miles can become more valuable. That’s because cardholders get at least 10% off award tickets that are operated by United or United Express. If you have United status, that discount gets bumped up to at least 15% off.

With the credit card, you have access to priority boarding in Group 2. That means you’ll be able to board earlier compared to the rest of the basic economy passengers in Group 6, making it more likely you’ll find space for your carry-on bag.

Now, you might be thinking: Wait a minute… Basic economy doesn’t allow you to bring a carry-on bag. Let me explain how that works.

United enforces its full-size carry-on restriction based on your boarding group. Group 6 passengers can't bring a full-size carry-on.

Because the credit card gets you Group 2 boarding, you essentially skip that restriction.

Premier members — who board in Group 2 or earlier — are also exempt from the full-size carry-on restriction when flying basic economy.

If you don’t want to deal with the hassle of a carry-on bag, you can opt to check it instead.

As long as you pay for your ticket using your United℠ Explorer Card, you’ll be able to check your first bag — and your companion’s first bag — for free when traveling on United. (If you’re booking an award ticket, make sure to use your card to pay for the taxes and fees.)

Keep in mind that if the first flight on your itinerary is operated by another airline, that airline’s baggage rules would apply and you would have to pay for your bag.

Of course, holding the right United credit card only gets you so far.

With basic economy, you’ll still need to pay a fee to change or cancel your ticket, and you won’t be able to select a seat for free.

Ultimately, whether basic economy is a good deal depends on a few factors.

If your plans might change, pay up for standard economy. Otherwise, the penalty to change or cancel will end up costing you more than you saved.

Another thing to consider is whether you’re willing to sit in a middle seat. You might be fine with it for a few hours, but what about a long-haul flight to Asia? Everyone’s threshold is different, so you’ll need to decide whether the middle-seat gamble is worth it.

If your plans are firm and you don’t mind a potential middle seat, booking a basic economy ticket can be a solid way to save money. Just book with a United card like, the United℠ Explorer Card, to avoid the biggest downsides.

#3158. Billionaire Investor Bill Ackman Just Issued a Blunt Warning to Wall Street

Ackman has emerged as one of the billionaire hedge fund managers the market pays attention to.

With more than three decades of investing experience, billionaire Bill Ackman runs Pershing Square Capital Management, which oversees about $33 billion across its funds and Howard Hughes Holdings, investing in equities through concentrated, bottom-up stock picking.

Ackman and his team have built a strong reputation as stock pickers, which is why investors are always curious to see what the billionaire investor and his team are investing in and what they think about the stock market.

Recently, Ackman appeared on CNBC and issued a blunt warning to Wall Street.

The stock market has experienced significant volatility in recent years, and it's not just because of artificial intelligence. Yes, a small group of AI stocks are now heavily weighted in the broader market S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%), so they do seem to have an outsize impact on the index.

But the stock market is vastly different from what it was, say, 10 or 20 years ago, because technology has given retail investors greater influence over investing and enabled practices like algorithmic trading, in which automated programs execute trades based on predefined conditions.

Furthermore, more people are passively invested and trained to buy the dip when stocks fall, creating another interesting dynamic in the market. Finally, there are additional financial instruments that allow investors to make short-term bets on the market or stocks, not to mention prediction markets.

"Every number of days, I feel like markets are broken," Ackman told CNBC on Nov. 3. "Stocks trade at prices that make no sense to me. Yes, it's good if you're a long-term investor and you can buy at a stupid price. I don't think it's good for the country generally."

"We're back to the casino-type markets when there was 95% leverage," Ackman added. "I don't think that's inherently good for the economy, for society, and it's leading to these massive moves in stocks."

Ackman has taken advantage of large, short-term declines in some of the world's largest tech and AI companies, purchasing shares of companies like Amazon and Microsoft when the market turned bearish.

Ackman purchased Amazon after it sold off in 2025 following President Donald Trump's announcement regarding large tariff hikes on most of the country's largest trading partners. Meanwhile, he purchased Microsoft earlier this year when the stock struggled amid concerns about AI's impact on the business.

Ackman believes people are taking on too much risk and trying to get rich quick, which often ends badly.

Ackman's warning rings true for both retail and institutional investors. Retail investors making big bets and trading on a near-term basis tend to suffer disastrous consequences.

A Schroder's study published in 2020, looking at over 148 years of data on the S&P 500 and its predecessors, found that investors who invested for only a month would have lost money roughly 40% of the time in inflation-adjusted terms.

On the institutional side, investors must remember the significant role consumers play in the U.S. economy, accounting for over two-thirds of spending. In the U.S., consumer health is absolutely vital. With more people investing and the market having rocketed higher in recent years, many have seen their wealth increase.

While it's true the wealthiest Americans still own the bulk of stocks, the bottom half of U.S. households have also benefited.

"With equities as the catalyst, the bottom half has seen its wealth grow nearly twice as fast as the top half across the 25 quarters of the current cycle encompassing the COVID recession and subsequent ongoing expansion," BCA Research's chief investment strategist Doug Peta wrote in a research note back in June, according to Barron's.

So, if this group starts to struggle due to market performance or risky behavior, it could impact the entire economy and, in turn, the entire stock market. That could explain why Ackman is concerned, despite these wild market swings creating investment opportunities for his funds.

#3156. The AI Control Gap: Companies Adopting AI Must Learn What Wall Street Learned The Hard Way

Samuel Kaluvuri, CEO of ApyHub, works on API infrastructure and runtime policy enforcement and holds a PhD in security assurance.

Somewhere inside a large bank, an AI agent has a name, a login ID and a manager who has to write its performance review.

This is less eccentric than it sounds, and it’s one of the more rational things I believe banking has done this year. These are institutions with serious risk functions and long memories for things that lose money quickly. Looking for a way to control software that acts on its own, they reached for the instruments they trusted: an identity, a reporting line and someone answerable for it.​

They are developing ways to manage a new kind of software, and the questions they are working through are ones other companies adopting agentic AI will increasingly need to address.​​

Enterprise software has always come with controls: permissions, approval chains, segregation of duties and audit logs. That worked for 30 years because a person asked for something, another looked at it and the system did exactly what was approved.

All three assumptions have stopped being true. The requester is now software operating at machine speed, and approval no longer describes the action. When someone signs off on “handle customer onboarding,” nothing in that sentence says which systems get touched, what data leaves which jurisdiction or what the agent does when it meets a case nobody thought about. The approval covers intent, but the risk lives in the path.

Put an approval workflow in front of a system taking thousands of autonomous actions, and you have not built oversight. You have built a very fast queue of things you already agreed to.

Finance learned this the hard (and expensive) way. Sign-off on trades worked until trades stopped happening at human speed. In 2012, Knight Capital pushed faulty code into production and lost more than $460 million in 45 minutes. By the time a conventional approval process notices a problem like that, the money is gone.

The response was not a better approval workflow. Control moved into the execution path: limits enforced before an order left the building, kill switches and real-time surveillance. Regulators then went further, and this is the part I believe is worth borrowing. Under the Securities and Exchange Commission’s market access rule, those controls must sit under the firm’s direct and exclusive control.

A broker may buy the risk technology from a third party, but it must keep the ability to monitor and adjust the controls in real time and cannot simply rely on the provider’s assurance that they work. The point of intervention moved to where the machine acts and stayed with whoever carries the liability.

So where does control over an agent actually live?

Not in the model. It sits below where these products are demonstrated and sold, in the software that determines which systems an agent can reach, what it may do with them, when it stops and what gets written down. Change the model, and the agent gets cleverer. Change that control layer, and it can no longer touch your payments system.

Three capabilities determine how effective these controls are: the ability to limit an agent’s actions before they happen, stop them while they are underway and independently reconstruct what the agent did afterward.​​

Running infrastructure that sits in the path of these calls gives you a different view. Human traffic arrives one action at a time. Agent traffic arrives in bursts: dozens of calls in a few seconds while the thing works through a task. Everyone can check whether the task completed, but few see what it read on the way or where it sent what it found.​

This is where the buying decision becomes important. A company does not necessarily have to hand this layer to its vendor. An enterprise can retain control over its access policies, gateways, transaction limits and logging, as many already do for systems used by employees. But those controls need to be deliberately extended to cover agents. Otherwise, buyers may inherit runtime rules configured by engineers focused on task completion or rely on defaults that are rarely revisited. These settings may also fall outside the governance documents boards and compliance teams regularly review.​

An employee’s limits are typically enforced through systems the bank controls and can adjust as needs change. An agent’s limits depend on the systems governing its actions, which may be managed by the buyer, the vendor or both. If the buyer has not established who controls that layer, important decisions may effectively be made elsewhere. The purchase is therefore not just software that performs tasks; it also involves a set of operating rules, some of which may already be in place before the buyer evaluates them.​

Platforms should be assessed not only on what an agent can do in a demonstration but also on where controls are enforced and who can change them. If a platform does not provide the necessary oversight, building a replacement layer may be one option, but it is not always practical or sufficient. In some cases, the better decision may be to keep a workflow under human supervision until the organization can establish controls appropriate for autonomous operation. That may be a less appealing sales proposition, but it can be the more responsible choice.​​​​

The regulatory direction is visible. In June 2026, the Financial Stability Board warned that the autonomy of AI agents can amplify risks that materialize at great speed.

Supervisors are no more likely to accept “our vendor handles that” than they were for outsourced trading infrastructure. Meanwhile, the platforms are sold on handing the work off entirely.

Every autonomous system runs inside rules that determine what it can do, and those rules exist whether or not the board has seen them. The question for a vendor is not merely who wrote them but whether you can inspect them, change them and, when the machine is already moving, enforce them yourself.​

#3154. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) Recently Crashed Out of the $1 Trillion Club. Should You Buy the Dip?

AMD just reported another blockbuster set of quarterly operating results, but they might not be enough to lift its stock in the near term.

The U.S. is currently home to 12 publicly listed companies worth $1 trillion or more. Semiconductor giant Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +11.04%) joined that exclusive club in September, but its stock has since declined by 25% from its peak, so the company is now valued at just $797 billion (as of the market close on Nov. 4).

AMD has become one of Nvidia's (NVDA +2.77%) top competitors in the market for data center graphics processing units (GPUs), which are the primary chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) workloads. Concerns about the sustainability of the AI infrastructure spending boom sparked the downside in AMD stock, but the company's operating results for the third quarter (ended Sept. 30) suggest sales won't be slowing down anytime soon.

Is this the ultimate buying opportunity for investors?

AMD launched its first dedicated AI data center GPU in 2023, and it was called the MI300X. It lagged Nvidia's original H100 GPU in terms of performance, but major tech companies like Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and Oracle thought it was a good alternative in the face of industrywide supply shortages.

AMD has since launched several new generations of its flagship GPU, and it has closed the gap to the competition. The company says its latest MI450 Series chips can be 15% more powerful and 30% more energy efficient than anything else on the market when installed in its fully integrated Helios data center rack. Helios includes specialized central processing units (CPUs), high-bandwidth memory, and networking components to extract the most processing power from every GPU.

AMD started shipping MI455X GPUs and Helios racks to a star-studded list of customers during the third quarter, which included Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle. OpenAI and Meta each plan to deploy 6 gigawatts' worth of computing capacity over the next few years using AMD's chips, and while they are starting with the MI450 Series, they will be big buyers of every future generation that follows.

In fact, AMD is already engaging customers regarding the MI500 Series and MI600 Series, which will deliver further leaps in performance.

AMD generated $13.4 billion in revenue across its three core business segments during the third quarter, which was a 45% increase from the year-ago period. But the data center segment alone accounted for $8.5 billion of that total, and it grew by a whopping 97%.

AMD chief executive Lisa Su believes data center sales will more than double in 2027, and will account for 80% of the company's total revenue. According to a series of comments last month, Su plans to substantially increase GPU supply next year to facilitate her strong growth forecast, suggesting the company might be gearing up to take market share from its competitors.

On the whole, Su's commentary alleviates recent fears that data center spending is poised for a slowdown, at least for now.

AMD delivered adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings of $6.65 per share over the last four quarters, placing its stock at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 73.5. That means it's almost three-times as expensive as Nvidia, which has a P/E ratio of 25.3.

Even if we value AMD stock based on Wall Street's average 2027 earnings estimate of $16.27 per share (provided by Yahoo! Finance), its stock has a forward P/E of 30. Therefore, even if the stock does absolutely nothing for the next 12 months, it will still be more expensive than Nvidia stock is today.

Therefore, AMD is basically priced for perfection heading into next year, leaving no room for error. If the company doesn't grow its data center business as fast as Su forecasted, its stock could suffer an even further decline.

As a result, it might not be wise to buy AMD stock at the current price. A return to the exclusive $1 trillion club might be possible in the future, but I think its valuation will be a barrier in the near term.

#3153. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3151. We Write About Saving Money; Here’s How We Trick Our Brains Into Doing It

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Even personal finance writers and editors need psychological hacks to save money. Here are the tips we use, and why they work.

While staring at the Container Store cart on my phone at 11 p.m., I did something for the first time that I’d read about a hundred times. Instead of spending $200 on more organizational boxes that I categorically did not need, I transferred that amount to my savings account.

Normally, my willpower is no match for the very real psychological phenomenon called present bias: Our brains light up more when we’re rewarding our current selves than our future selves.

Research has also shown that you imagine your future self almost like a stranger — it’s tougher to care about that stranger than about who you are right now. But that night, I saw near-future-me using that $200 on next summer’s vacation. I wanted the vacation more than the boxes. So I abandoned my cart.

I had managed to use a psychological savings trick: Find a goal that helps you envision your future self. With this epiphany in mind, I asked some of my fellow Nerds to share the savings habits they’ve put to work in their own lives. Perhaps reading these can give late-night you some saving inspiration.

Kimberly Palmer, senior writer and spokesperson: I let nonessential items sit in my online shopping cart for at least 24 hours before buying them. It definitely makes me realize I don't need a lot of them! I also informed my children of this rule, and it has helped cut down on their requests — or at least they know they have to be patient.

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: Fellow let-it-sit-in-the-cart person here. I wait for notifications that something's at least 30% off before I make any moves. Ideally, 40% to 50% off.

Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor: When I browse online, I add an item to my shopping cart and wait 24 to 48 hours. After that, I either decide it’s a waste of money/an impulse purchase and delete it from my cart (or forget about the cart altogether), or I decide I want it and make the purchase — it’s the former 99% of the time.

Why it works: “Waiting 1 to 2 days allows me to take the emotion out of purchasing. I no longer succumb to marketing or sales, and instead make spending decisions based on what my family and I actually need or can use.” — Julie again, eloquently making the point for me.

Caitlin Constantine, managing editor: My one real shopping weakness is books, and I’ve found I can get a very close approximation of that feeling without spending an outrageous amount of money by going to the library, wandering around the stacks to see what books might look interesting, and checking out a bunch of them. Even if I don’t end up reading them, I’m still helping the library with circulation numbers, so I see it as a win-win.

Spencer Tierney, senior writer: Plus one to Caitlin Constantine’s “my one real shopping weakness is books.” If I want an older or smaller book, I'll try to find it at one of four libraries I belong to on Libby, the library e-book reader app. (The Libby waitlist for new books can take months, so I have to account for that.)

Why it works: There’s no secret here: It’s nice to get free stuff. You might be surprised what the library has to offer, like movies, magazine subscriptions, games, classes and theater tickets.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: We always tell people to automate savings, and I do in my high-yield savings account, but Dasha Kennedy, the woman behind “The Broke Black Girl”, told Elizabeth Ayoola on the Smart Money podcast that you should invest, even a little bit every week or so, for future you. So I just set up a small recurring deposit to my robo-advisor.

Why it works: You only have to make this decision once for your future self, not over and over again. And if you do it early enough, you could avoid being part of the 41% of Americans who wish they had started investing earlier, according to a 2026 NerdWallet survey.

Athena Cocoves, managing editor: To cut down on food delivery, I started cooking when I feel like it instead of when I’m supposed to. I exercise free will and make soup at 10 p.m. It sounds more obvious than it feels, and it's made a big difference in my budget. And it'd make an even bigger difference if I wasn't also rewarding myself with fancy spices and vinegars, but a girl's gotta splurge somehow.

Ryan Brady, lead writer: My wife takes advantage of a T-Mobile freebie that gives us a discount for DoorDash deliveries. She uses it to buy groceries from Aldi instead of takeout. Aldi is far from us. Publix is right across the street, but more expensive. So this saves us money on the actual items and also helps us not impulse buy (as we often do when we're in-store shopping).

Why it works: You don’t need to call on willpower if you can avoid the situation that tempts you to spend money.

» Read more: Strategies to save on groceries that actually work

Kenley Young, managing editor: I use credit cards for most purchases to get those sweet, sweet rewards, but there's a lot in this article that I've also taken to heart.

I've started using library resources more, and it's saving me money on things like monthly subscriptions.

I've negotiated down several monthly bills, too: refinanced my car loan, got cheaper homeowners insurance, opted for a little less auto coverage in exchange for a lower premium, and haggled online with everyone from Xfinity and SiriusXM to my local newspaper until they all gave me a discount.

Plus, I've opted for some home improvement projects with the expectation that my utility bills would be lower. A plumber finally fixed our toilet, which has led to lower water bills, and I even installed solar panels.

Lastly, my analog skill (playing live music) has become a steady side hustle. I play eight to 10 gigs a month, where (on top of my baseline rate) I also get tips, free food and beer.

Why it works: Because you’re Kenley and you put in a lot of effort.

But you don’t need to be Kenley to find a savings habit that works for your personality, your financial situation and even your musical talents. You just need to experiment. Pick the strategy that speaks to you most, and test it out. Which one are you going to try first?

#3149. 2 Brilliant Stocks to Buy in November and Hold Forever

Shopify and Duolingo both just posted strong third-quarter results, and each looks built to compound for years.

Buying a stock to hold forever doesn't mean forgetting about the business. It means holding on as long as the investment case holds up.

Shopify (SHOP +3.59%) and Duolingo (DUOL +2.17%) just showed that case getting stronger, with strong third-quarter financial results. These leaders in e-commerce and mobile learning are building momentum heading into 2027, making them timely growth stocks to buy in November and hold for potentially a lifetime of compounding returns.

Shopify provides the software that merchants use to run their entire business, both online and in stores. Once a company's products, orders, and customers are running on Shopify, switching is costly and disruptive. In 2026, Shopify has proven it can be a major beneficiary of more people using artificial intelligence (AI) to find things to buy.

Its gross merchandise volume (GMV), the total value of sales on its platform, grew 30% year over year last quarter to about $119 billion. That's the sixth straight quarter at this level of growth.

AI agents are opening up a whole new channel in commerce. President Harley Finkelstein said AI traffic to Shopify merchants rose 2.6 times over the prior year, and orders grew 3.3 times.

That's why management sees AI as a growth driver. Finkelstein called agentic shopping "an incremental increase to commerce." Shopify is showing it can adapt to technological shifts to help its merchants grow their businesses, which is why this is a business built to compound over decades.

As of midday trading on Nov. 4, the stock's price-to-free cash flow multiple is about 85, which looks expensive but within the stock's historical range. It's a platform merchants depend on, and it appears to be gaining even more relevance in this new AI era. That's a growth stock investors can hold for years.

Duolingo is the world's leading mobile learning platform, with nearly 65 million daily active users. It turns learning into a game by rewarding users with streaks and other incentives to encourage them to open the app every day.

That daily engagement feeds a data advantage. "Nobody has the amount of data of people learning that we do," CEO Luis von Ahn said. Duolingo runs hundreds of tests every week to improve the app, and he credits most of its user gains to better retention.

The results are showing. Daily active users (DAUs) grew 29% year over year last quarter, up from 23% in Q2 and 21% in Q1. Bookings growth followed, accelerating to 12% from 8%, and management raised its full-year guidance.

The runway is long. "Our ambition is to ultimately reach 1 billion learners and build a much larger business over time," von Ahn said. About 1 billion people are learning math worldwide, he noted, and chess just hit 10 million daily users while remaining "completely under-monetized."

The stock traded at about 21 times trailing free cash flow, at the $168 share price on Nov. 4. A learning app that people open every day and that adapts to each person is a compounder worth holding for the long haul.

#3148. Why The Same Threat Means Different Things To Different Companies

Anuj Goel is CEO and co-founder of Cyware, a company focused on intelligence-led cybersecurity and operational resilience.

Every threat intelligence feed shares a blind spot: It knows the threat but nothing about our specific environment.

The feed carries threat data; only our environment provides context. The industry has spent a decade refining data when it should have focused on environment-specific context.

As a practitioner, the hardest conversations were never about explaining suspicious activity. They were about explaining why it reached us when the best intelligence available had already flagged it. We had the indicators. We just weren’t connecting them to the assets they might reach. What surprised me then, and still does, is that the problem was never a shortage of intelligence or its accuracy. It was the missing step between knowing about a threat and knowing, in real time, that it applied to us. That experience shaped how I think about this space, and it is why I believe context, not volume, is where the real work is.

Intelligence has no universal version; “good intelligence” depends on sector and geography, not sheer volume.

Financial institutions require fraud-focused reporting, while industrial operators need OT intelligence built around controllers and plant-floor realities. Neither is “better,” but they aren’t interchangeable. Relevance is inherently specific to who we are and where we operate.

No feed can see inside our walls, and that’s where we decide which known threats matter to our environment.

Relevance is derived from the assets we actually run. The identities and access paths that connect them. What is business-critical versus incidental? Where our controls are strong and where they are thin. This is the ground truth every external indicator has to be measured against. An indicator evaluated against our environment becomes elevated to a prioritized, actionable risk. The same indicator, without an environment behind it, is just a rumor about someone else’s network.

Relevance is the product of the two: the intelligence our sector trusts, correlated with the infrastructure, data and assets we have. Neither input alone produces it. The best feeds in the world, unmeasured against our environment, cannot tell us what to do first on Monday morning. A perfect map of our environment, with no sector intelligence flowing into it, has nothing to act on either.

Consider when identical intelligence arrives at two different organizations.

For one, the indicator maps to a critical, internet-facing application reachable by elevated identities. This context resolves to a high-urgency risk, requiring immediate isolation and escalation.

For the second, the same indicator maps to a decommissioned service or a segment with existing controls. This context resolves to a low-urgency risk requiring only logging.

Same feed. Same indicator. Same morning. Two entirely different answers, and two entirely different actions determined by adding the context.

This is what customer-specific context means in practice. It is not a cleaner presentation of the same data. It is a different computed result for every organization, because the inputs on the other side of the equation differ for every organization. It determines not only whether to act, but what action is warranted, in what order and with how much confidence. Any system that skips this step applies one global severity score to environments that share almost nothing in common.

One line is worth drawing sharply, because the industry constantly blurs it. Tagging an indicator as malicious is enrichment, attaching a known attribute to a piece of data. Knowing that the same indicator belongs to a campaign actively targeting our sector, that a machine on our finance team touched it three days ago and that the identity behind that machine is exposed, that is context. Enrichment adds metadata. Context fuels risk reduction.

This is also why dozens of feeds never added up to an answer. More raw indicators, unmeasured against our environment, is a larger pile to triage, not a clearer picture. Most security leaders have a graveyard of unused subscriptions to prove it.

Increasingly, the systems making security decisions are not human analysts reading a feed. They are platforms and agents consuming intelligence to prioritize, correlate and act, and a decision engine is only as good as what we put into it.

Feed a system raw, one-size-fits-all intelligence and it inherits the problem we started with: It cannot tell a live risk from an irrelevant one, because the feed never carried that distinction. The input has to be measured against that specific environment, already resolved into what is relevant, exposed and worth acting on.

This reframes what “having threat intelligence” should mean. A feed is not the same as threat context, and a raw feed piped into a decision-making tool does not become context on arrival. Intelligence has to be made relevant before it becomes an input, per sector, per environment, per organization or every tool consuming it is reasoning from a rumor.

The organizations—and increasingly, the systems—best positioned for what is coming are not the ones holding the most feeds. Instead, the organizations receiving actionable context are those that understand what threat intelligence means for them and are equipped to drive necessary security actions.​​

#3146. Donald Trump's Investment Team Sold Micron. Here's What Investors Should Know Before Following the Money.

Trump's team dumped Micron, but that's no reason for you to follow.

There has been a "Trump dump" of Micron Technology (MU +5.12%) stock. Federal financial disclosures recently revealed that President Donald Trump's brokerage accounts sold between $251,000 and $515,000 of the tech stock in August.

Anytime a prominent figure buys or sells a significant amount of any stock, it often attracts attention. That's true even in a case like this, where it was actually the president's investment team that made the call to sell Micron, rather than Trump himself.

Should retail investors sell Micron, too? Here's what you need to know first.

The most important thing to understand is that Trump's sale of Micron stock wasn't a major story. You might even call it a "nothingburger." The move appeared to be a simple case of profit-taking. Micron's shares were up more than 750% over the previous 12 months when the president's team sold the stock.

Another reason investors shouldn't put too much focus on any of the president's portfolio transactions is that they don't necessarily reflect much, if anything, about the merits of an individual stock. Trump's investment advisors likely balance multiple factors, including diversification and liquidity needs, tax planning, and more, that sometimes require selling solid stocks.

Arguably, the biggest issue with blindly following trades made by Trump's team is the time lag. Presidential financial disclosures are only required within 45 days of a trade (plus an annual disclosure). By the time they're filed, a lot could have changed with any given stock bought or sold during the period. The same premise applies to copying trades made by members of the U.S. Congress.

Granted, the decision by President Trump's team to sell Micron stock appears smart in retrospect. The stock has fallen sharply since the large sale on Aug. 21, 2026. However, Micron's fundamentals remain exceptionally strong.

The company's revenue soared 31% quarter over quarter and 379% year over year in its fiscal fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 3, 2026. Earnings jumped 38.5% quarter over quarter and 11.8x year over year.

Sure, Micron is a cyclical stock. But its boom cycle is showing no signs of slowing down. COO Manish Bhatia said in the fourth-quarter earnings call that the company is "seeing stronger demand drivers than we've seen before" for both 2027 and 2028. He noted that Micron has "more than 75% of our shipments committed for the year" for fiscal 2027.

As hyperscalers ramp up their artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, the demand for memory chips continues to surge. That's especially the case for high-bandwidth memory (HBM). And Micron is a key leader in the global HBM market.

Meanwhile, the stock looks dirt cheap on multiple widely used valuation metrics. Micron's shares trade below five times forward earnings. Its price-to-earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio, which factors in analysts' five-year earnings growth projections, is a super-low 0.16.

Of the 28 Wall Street analysts who have rated Micron over the past three months, all but one recommended buying shares. The lone outlier advised investors to hold the stock.

Even more impressive, the average Wall Street 12-month price target for Micron implies roughly 130% upside. The most pessimistic price target for the stock is around 70% above the share price as of Nov. 5, 2026.

Should investors buy Micron based on analysts' enthusiasm about the stock? The answer is a resounding "no." It's important to make your own investment decisions independently of political figures' moves or the consensus view on Wall Street.

That said, Micron's recent sell-off could present a buying opportunity for investors who think it will take a while for the supply demand imbalance in memory chips to be resolved.

#3143. Is Alphabet's Core Search Business in Trouble? Looking Past the Headline Revenue Growth Provides a Clear Answer.

Slowing sales growth has investors worried about Alphabet's cash cow.

Investors did not like what Alphabet (GOOG +0.78%) (GOOGL +0.78%) management had to say when it announced its third-quarter earnings. While the company's massive cash burn gets all the attention as it builds more data centers to meet demand from AI developers, its cash cow, Google Search, has also raised some red flags.

The Search business saw revenue growth decelerate sharply last quarter, climbing just 12% year over year, compared to 17% growth in the second quarter. Management warned that revenue growth could remain under pressure in the fourth quarter. That's led many to conclude that the rise of AI is finally starting to affect Alphabet's main profit center, which makes its massive AI build-out much riskier.

Investors need to dig deeper than the headline numbers to determine exactly what's going on here. Here's what management had to say and what it means for patient, long-term investors.

Even as Google Search revenue growth is slowing, people are using it more and more. Management reported the highest year-over-year growth in search queries in the last five years. Management also said the way people use Search is changing. "Their queries are longer, personalized and multimodal," CEO Sundar Pichai said during the company's third-quarter earnings call.

That means users are providing a ton of details about exactly what they're looking for using text, voice, photos, and other uploads to Google. Those details can be extremely valuable, as they can ultimately facilitate better ad targeting for users.

Alphabet has successfully leveraged generative artificial intelligence on the business-facing side of Search, making it easier for businesses to create and target ad campaigns to maximize value. As more search engagement shifts to Google's AI Mode and other new interfaces, it's only a matter of time before it finds the right product fit to maximize the value of its engagement and the valuable data its users provide for advertising.

In fact, investors might not have to wait long to see revenue reaccelerate. Management said it's already scaling efforts to show ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, bringing the ad load more in line with traditional Search. "[O]ur user research shows that people are comfortable with ads on these surfaces and find them highly relevant," Philipp Schindler, Senior Vice President and Chief Business Officer at Google, said during the earnings call.

In the meantime, Alphabet is bringing more AI features with potential monetization paths to where its users are already highly engaged. It's rolling out more agentic AI features directly in AI Mode in Google Search, after finding success with them in the Gemini app (which is used by 1 billion people). "One area I'm excited about is helping people get things done, be it booking reservations, filling in forms, scheduling appointments, or making purchases," Pichai said. Most of those examples open the door for more monetization opportunities.

While it's worth paying attention to the developments at Google Search, looking beyond the headline number to see how engagement and monetization plans are changing for the product is more important. The outlook for the business remains strong, and the slowdown in revenue growth will likely be more gradual than the previous quarter suggests, with occasional ups and downs over the next few quarters as it scales monetization across new surfaces.

The Search business also shouldn't distract from the big growth story at Alphabet: Google Cloud Platform. Overall cloud computing revenue more than doubled last quarter with strong margin expansion. While management expects some margin pressure in the next few quarters as it uses more third-party compute capacity, the business should see considerable revenue growth. The returns on its massive investments in new data centers appear well worth the cost, as Google Cloud is set to surpass Search as the largest driver of operating income growth in 2027. That said, Search is no slouch in that department.

The near-term pressure on the stock price appears to be an excellent buying opportunity for patient investors. Shares now trade at less than 19 times forward earnings expectations, indicating declining confidence in the company's growth prospects. But the underlying data suggest its cash cow is in good shape, and its biggest growth driver is on track to deliver excellent returns for shareholders.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 6.96% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is five basis points lower than yesterday and 11 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

The recent slide in mortgage rates might reverse course if next week’s inflation data comes in hot.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday, Nov. 10. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at the other data set, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn healthy: The October jobs report, released today from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Right now, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as expected and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates will be less affected.

Under-the-radar tech stock Blackbaud (BLKB -3.01%) had an October to remember. It added that the service is "designed to help customers identify opportunities faster, make more informed decisions and act with greater confidence."

If performance at least matches its promise, this unified AI architecture will not only be a highly useful, cutting-edge suite; it will also stand a good chance of becoming a go-to system for nonprofits and related institutions. And a strong niche product can be hard to beat.

#3137. Closing The Enterprise AI Security Gap: From Blind Spots To Stronger Defenses

Vasanth Mudavatu, Senior Principal Software Engineer at a Fortune 50 company, dedicated to the security of generative AI and ML systems.

Enterprise AI security is no longer just about preventing inaccurate answers. It’s about preventing an automated system from using legitimate access to expose confidential information or execute unauthorized actions.

EchoLeak, which was disclosed in June 2025, was a Microsoft 365 Copilot vulnerability that allowed a crafted email to trigger data exfiltration without requiring the victim to click a malicious link. Microsoft assigned it a CVSS severity score of 9.3, while NIST separately rated it 7.5.

Microsoft patched the vulnerability, and no evidence of exploitation in the wild was reported. This was a demonstrated vulnerability rather than a confirmed breach, but it exposed a consequential failure: External content could influence a system operating with access to internal information.

If an AI agent put customer data, revenue or reputation at risk today, could your organization explain what happened and stop it before the damage spread? The answer depends less on reassuring model behavior than on enforceable boundaries.

The framework below connects four activities: assessing six security blind spots, prioritizing findings, implementing controls in phases and verifying that those controls work.

Attackers can automate reconnaissance, credential harvesting and data extraction. Enterprises need to examine both how AI can be attacked and how it can accelerate attacks.

Being aware of the following six blind spots turn that concern into an actionable security assessment:

A downloaded model shouldn’t become a trusted production asset simply because it comes from a familiar repository. Modified weights, backdoor triggers and unsafe model-file deserialization are areas requiring scrutiny.

Recommended controls include verifying artifact signatures and hashes, documenting provenance, scanning inbound files and testing model behavior before deployment. Integrity verification establishes whether an artifact matches an approved baseline; behavioral testing examines whether it performs as expected. Neither replaces the other.

Disabling an agent isn’t necessarily the same as removing its access. Credentials, active tokens and downstream permissions may remain usable.

Agents need distinct identities, least-privilege access and short-lived credentials, and revocation workflows should be tested. Assessment should also consider combined permissions across tools, as individually acceptable capabilities may collectively create an unacceptable access path.

A useful operational test is straightforward: Disable an agent and verify that its downstream actions actually stop.

Inspecting the final response covers only one potential exit point. Sensitive information may also appear in tool-call arguments, logs, traces or data written to vector stores.

Monitor these boundaries, restrict outbound destinations and correlate activity across requests. That correlation matters because information can leave in small fragments rather than one easily detected transfer.

The assessment should follow the complete data journey, not just the conversation visible to the user.

The security boundary includes more than the model. Build workflows, libraries, containers and deployment dependencies also require review.

Scan inbound model artifacts, pin third-party GitHub Actions to specific commit hashes and maintain an AI-specific inventory of model and software dependencies. These measures help teams identify what they deployed and investigate compromised components.

The objective is traceability, knowing which artifacts and dependencies support each production capability.

A compromised agent may use legitimate tools and credentials to interact with connected systems. Shared memory and agent-to-agent communication introduce additional paths through which malicious instructions can propagate.

Organizations should authenticate communication, verify message integrity, inspect memory and implement per-agent quarantine. Additionally, review Model Context Protocol tool metadata for adversarial instructions or unapproved changes.

Trust should be established at each boundary rather than inherited automatically from another agent.

An agent inventory must capture more than a name. Security teams need ownership, approved capabilities, authorization context and a defined retirement process.

Automate discovery, log audits at the action level and decommission workflows that revoke credentials, address retained memory and preserve required audit records. These controls connect governance decisions to what agents do.

A gap analysis becomes useful when it drives priorities. Evaluate risks using likelihood, impact, difficulty of detection and an exposure multiplier for multi-agent environments.

Treat the resulting score as a prioritization aid, not an objective prediction. Organizations should document their assumptions and calibrate escalation thresholds to their own systems and business consequences.

• The missing control and supporting evidence.

• The test that will demonstrate closure.

Don’t consider a control complete merely because a policy or configuration exists. Closure should require evidence that it works.

The roadmap begins with agent discovery, model integrity checks, outbound monitoring, pipeline hardening and kill-switch implementation. Subsequent phases introduce managed identities, behavioral testing, inter-agent authentication, memory inspection and automated response workflows.

This sequencing provides a practical starting point—establish visibility and containment first and then deepen prevention and detection.

The strongest contribution of this framework is its operational focus. It asks teams to connect model provenance, agent permissions, runtime activity and incident response rather than assess each in isolation.

Leadership reporting should emphasize measurable coverage and tested effectiveness. Useful measures include the proportion of agents under governance, model integrity verification coverage, supply chain scanning coverage and decommissioning compliance.

These measures should be considered alongside the evidence used to close individual findings, connecting implementation progress to demonstrated control effectiveness.

For enterprise leaders, the goal isn’t to eliminate every uncertainty before deploying AI. It’s to make that uncertainty manageable with accountable ownership, observable actions and tested intervention paths. Governance sets expectations; operational evidence shows whether the organization can enforce them.​

#3135. Could Investing $10,000 in IonQ Stock Make You a Millionaire?

IonQ has major growth potential, but a 100x return is a lot.

Investing in early-stage companies like IonQ (IONQ +23.42%) with major upside in the quantum computing space is an attractive proposition. If you pick the right stocks, it could provide life-changing returns. Some are even calling IonQ stock a millionaire-maker stock.

Could a $10,000 investment in IonQ really make you a millionaire? Let's take a look.

Turning a $10,000 investment into a $1 million sum requires finding a stock that can rise 100x. Few stocks in the market have done this, but there are several examples out there. However, history is not on IonQ's side. IonQ is currently a $10 billion company, so it would need to become a $1 trillion company to reach this goal. There aren't a ton of $1 trillion companies on the market, but the list is growing bigger each year.

One company fairly similar to IonQ that was valued at more than $1 trillion prior to selling off was AMD (AMD +11.04%). While AMD is valued at $762 billion now, it's a great stock to compare IonQ to because they both make computing units. Over the past 12 months, AMD's revenue has totaled over $40 billion.

So, for IonQ to get into the $1 trillion club, its revenue must reach that or even higher. McKinsey & Company estimates that the global quantum computing market could generate up to $72 billion annually by 2035, so if IonQ captures the whole market, this revenue figure isn't too far-fetched. However, capturing all of it will be a tall task, as there are several potent competitors with huge cash backing that could challenge IonQ in the quantum computing realm.

As a result, I don't think achieving a $1 trillion valuation is in the cards for IonQ anytime soon.

Furthermore, IonQ is a very high-risk company. Putting any more than 1% of your total portfolio into IonQ's stock would be very risky. If 1% of your portfolio equals $10,000, congratulations, you're already a millionaire!

So, can a $10,000 investment in IonQ make you a millionaire? I'd say no. Additionally, investing $10,000 in a much smaller portfolio than $1 million would be very risky and could have some major implications for your long-term returns if it doesn't work out. However, that doesn't mean IonQ is a bad investment -- just that investors need to temper their expectations.

#3133. 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow

Startups often move quickly because they have to, making the most of limited resources and adapting as circumstances change. As tech companies scale, added layers of process, approval and hierarchy can gradually slow decision making and erode the flexibility that helped them grow.

The good news is that companies don’t have to abandon the habits that fueled their early success as they expand. Here, Forbes Technology Council members share startup habits established tech companies should preserve—or relearn—to maintain their agility as they grow.

Established tech companies should preserve the startup habit of staying close to the raw customer experience. As organizations scale, dashboards and layers of interpretation can obscure what people actually struggle with. Leaders should keep speaking directly with customers and empower small teams to act quickly on what they learn. Scale should improve execution, not distance companies from users. - Leah Wang, Karpo

The tech market in the AI era is changing super fast—the cycles for product demands, work methods and tools, and customers’ needs and requirements have all become very short. The one thing companies must preserve is agility within the boundaries of their focus. It is easy to get lost and try to achieve everything, only to end up with nothing. Being able to stay agile while knowing the problem your company solves is critical. - Yoav Amitai, Elsight

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Startups are great at prototyping new products and services and moving on quickly from ideas during the research and development phase. As companies scale, this “create fast, test fast, decide fast” capacity is often diminished. One way to keep it alive is to engage early with a customer or partner to confirm requirements or do testing. It puts healthy pressure on the development process while gathering valuable external feedback on pricing, functionality and positioning. - Eva Rudin, Thales Cybersecurity

Preserve the willingness to challenge assumptions. Startups move quickly because they don’t treat “this is how it’s done” as an acceptable answer. As companies scale, process can quietly replace curiosity. The best teams keep questioning their own products, decisions and assumptions, especially when something appears to be working. Scale should give you more resources to challenge the status quo, not more reasons to protect it. - Alissa Knight, Assail, Inc.

Keep saying no to the wrong business. When you are small, you cannot serve everyone, so you get good at turning down the wrong customers and use cases, and that focus is half of why you survive. At scale, every deal looks worth taking, and the muscle for walking away weakens. You must protect it on purpose. The companies that keep rejecting what does not fit stay sharp long after they could afford to lose focus. - Vytautas Savickas, Oxylabs

Solve problems close to where they occur. As organizations scale, issues often get escalated to the most senior person rather than the person best connected to the customer or the detail of the issue. That introduces delays to fixes being made and promotes permission-seeking rather than judgment and accountability. Push authority down and let the people closest to the problem make the call. - Rob Sloan, Zscaler

Knowing when to stop is crucial. Startups have to focus because their resources are limited. The ability in a startup to know exactly what is going on means not only decisions to invest but also decisions to divest are made faster. - Véronique Özkaya, DATAmundi

AI-first thinking is the biggest thing established players need to adopt from the startup realm. New ventures have the luxury of AI being the starting point, not something they need to bolt onto old, outdated processes. That blank slate is a real edge—no legacy systems standing between them and AI-driven gains. So, I’d begin every problem by asking where AI can make the biggest impact and build from there. That mindset will define the future enterprise. - Tarek Nseir, Valliance

Preserve the habit of testing before debating. Startups rarely have enough data to eliminate uncertainty, so they build something small, put it in front of users, and learn. At scale, debate can become a substitute for discovery. Established companies should relearn how to turn unanswered questions into fast, low-risk experiments, using evidence from the market to resolve what meetings cannot. - Melissa King, Paylocity

Let the people closest to a problem try things without asking permission first. In many cases, our team members have made our most impactful suggestions. We discussed it, tried it out and looked at the results together. Nobody wrote a proposal. Give teams a sandbox, clear data and security rules, and a few weeks to test. You’ll learn more than you would from a six-month planning cycle. - Merav Yuravlivker, Data Society

Keep communication lines efficient. The best startups have an uncanny ability to throw unnecessary hierarchy to the wind and flatten communication lines. That’s how startups home in on solutions rather than simply admiring the problem. - James Stanger, CompTIA

Cross-department talk is essential. In a startup, everyone can talk to everyone without wondering about politics and the org chart. You never know where the next good idea will come from—it often comes from an “unexpected part” of the org chart. If Joe from team X is afraid of talking to Mary from team Y just because they don’t have the same boss, the company’s capacity to innovate is severely impacted. - Stephane Donze, AODocs

Startups move fast because they accept higher risk, while large organizations slow down to protect reputation, revenue and investors. As companies grow, they must consciously balance risk appetite to keep innovating. Teams should also keep the startup habit of “relentless iteration”—sharing early “sh***y first drafts,” as referenced by Brené Brown—for fast feedback instead of waiting for polish. - Mandy Andress, Elastic

Ship things that aren’t ready and learn from real users instead of extensive internal reviews. Process exists to prevent mistakes, but it also prevents speed and discovery. Talk directly to users without a layer of research, summaries or account managers in between. - Amy Gu, Dynamsoft

Create rituals early and maintain them throughout your growth. Startup life is hard. One of the things that inspires and preserves team alignment is the rituals created in early startup life that create an identity, a battle cry and a touchstone to the mission. As new employees join the company, these same rituals become part of their orientation, which helps encourage unity. - Amy Brown, Authenticx

Preserve fast, reversible decision making. Let teams run small, bounded tests without routing every choice through layers of approval, then use the results to adjust quickly. Reserve heavyweight reviews for decisions that are costly or difficult to undo—not every experiment. - Nagesh Nama, xLM Continuous Intelligence

Share the full picture with everyone. In a startup, the whole team knows the revenue, the biggest customer problem, and what worries the founders most. As companies grow, that context gets held back at the top, and teams start working on tasks without knowing why they matter. People make better decisions when they know what the company is facing. - Asad Khan, TestMu AI

Preserve the startup habit of a hard work-in-progress limit. Early teams cannot pursue 20 “top priorities,” so starting one thing means stopping another. At scale, portfolios expand faster than capacity, and coordination becomes the bottleneck. Force every new priority to displace an old one. Speed comes as much from limiting concurrency as from moving faster. - Akhilesh Sharma, A3Logics Inc.

Do it by hand before automating it. Startups run a new process manually for a few weeks and learn where it actually breaks. Larger companies jump straight to automation and lock in their guesses. In mature organizations we audit, roughly a third of flows either duplicate another or barely run. A month of manual work first is cheaper than a year of maintaining the wrong automation. - Sergii Grushai, Peeklogic

#3132. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3130. 3 Internet Giants to Hold for the Next 10 Years

The Nasdaq slipped last month on AI spending concerns, but these tech stocks still deliver useful services to the masses every day.

The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.09%) is down about 5% since the end of September, as of Nov. 2, 2026. The sell-off comes as Wall Street worries about big tech's spending on artificial intelligence (AI). But leading tech stocks remain some of the best ways to build wealth over the long term.

Over the last 10 years, Alphabet (GOOGL +0.78%) (GOOG +0.78%), Amazon (AMZN -0.35%), and Netflix (NFLX -3.28%) each grew revenue at least fivefold, and hundreds of millions of people use their services daily. Each is benefiting from AI, making them three of the best internet giants to hold for the next 10 years. Here's why they are worth buying now for the long term.

Alphabet runs Google Search and YouTube, and its Gemini app just hit 1 billion users. Yet the stock is down 19% since Sept. 30, trailing the Nasdaq. That dip could be an opportunity, since fears that AI chatbots will replace Google may be overblown.

AI is actually helping Alphabet grow Search ad revenue. During the third-quarter earnings call, CEO Sundar Pichai said query growth is the fastest in five years, partly driven by increasing usage of AI Mode, Google's chatbot-style search feature. Now Google is rolling out AI Mode ads globally, giving it more search queries to monetize.

Growing usage of AI features helped push Search revenue up 12% year over year to $63 billion last quarter. Pichai said the trust Google has built "with scale in billions of users" will "end up being a huge differentiator" in AI.

One risk is that AI Mode ads currently earn less per search, which management said weighed on results. Still, the stock looks reasonably priced at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 18 times 2027 earnings estimates, below its five-year average trailing P/E of about 24, and analysts expect about 17% annual earnings growth over the next five years.

Amazon leads online shopping with hundreds of millions of Prime members and also leads the cloud computing market with Amazon Web Services (AWS). The stock is down just 0.9% since Sept. 30 and up 7% year-to-date as of Nov. 2.

AI is a big opportunity for these businesses. More than 400 million customers used Alexa for Shopping, Amazon's agentic AI assistant, in the past year, and U.S. users spend 50% more per order. In AWS, revenue commitments for its Graviton and Trainium chips each rose more than 20 times year over year, and customers using them saved more than $2 billion last quarter. Those savings are why companies stick with AWS.

CEO Andy Jassy believes AWS can deliver 40% annualized growth through 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years. AWS growth helped Amazon post its highest operating margin ever last quarter.

The risk is spending: Amazon's capital spending hit $77 billion last quarter, pushing free cash flow (cash from operations minus capital expenditures) to negative $47 billion on a trailing-12-month basis. If demand for AWS slowed, that spending could take longer to pay off.

Still, at about 23 times 2027 earnings estimates, Amazon stock trades at a reasonable price relative to growth expectations, with analysts expecting about 23% annual earnings growth.

Netflix has more than 325 million paid memberships, serving an audience approaching 1 billion people. Yet the stock is down 10.6% since Sept. 30 and 33% year-to-date, which could be a buying opportunity.

AI helps Netflix serve that audience at lower cost. Generative AI tools helped make about 300 titles this year, speeding up production and cutting costs. AI also help members find shows they'll like, which can contribute to lower cancellations and greater customer satisfaction.

A risk is that viewing hours rose just 2% in the first half of 2026. Management said it needs more global hits to lift that number. If it doesn't execute on its content slate, it could be harder to grow revenue. Still, the stock trades at about 17 times next year's earnings estimates -- a modest valuation with analysts still expecting about 21% annual earnings growth.

Tech stocks might remain volatile in the near term. But as people continue to search, shop, and stream every day, Alphabet, Amazon, and Netflix will benefit and continue to grow in value for the next 10 years and beyond.

#3127. Elon Musk Wants to Build an "Enormous Robot Army." Here's What That Means for Tesla and SpaceX Investors.

Elon Musk is fighting for complete control of Tesla's voting power.

Last year, Elon Musk stressed his priority of regaining majority voting control over Tesla (TSLA +4.23%). His biggest concern at the time was control over new products -- humanoid robots, in particular -- that Tesla is expected to produce en masse over the coming years.

"My fundamental concern with regard to how much voting control I have in Tesla is: If I go ahead and build this enormous robot army, can I just be ​ousted at some point in the future?" Musk told investors last October.

Whether investors agree with Musk's concern or not, it is clear that he seeks majority control over Tesla's daily operations. This has one major implication for shareholders of both Tesla and SpaceX (SPCX +8.62%).

While a merger between SpaceX and Tesla has not been formally announced, speculation of a potential tie-up has risen sharply after the companies launched independent committees focused on exploring the benefits of a merger.

Musk's negotiated pay package at Tesla originally included key milestones that would trigger additional stock grants, including the deployment of one million humanoid robots. But some experts are claiming that Musk's ambitious "enormous robot army" is a distraction from his true goal.

"It's irrelevant," Charles Elson, ​founding director of the Weinberg Center, told Reuters this week. "This package is a distraction from the real story, which is complete control."

Musk's pay package with SpaceX grants him additional voting power before the shares are even issued. Incorporating the new pay package, Musk now has approximately 85% voting power at SpaceX. With roughly 20% voting power at Tesla, a tie-up between the two companies could ultimately give Musk majority control over the combined entity.

SpaceX's IPO prospectus was replete with bold long-term plans. Tesla, meanwhile, is working to sustain its lofty valuation with promises of robot armies and ubiquitous self-driving cars. Investors, however, should look deeper into these claims, understanding that a mega-merger between Tesla and SpaceX may have more to do with Musk's economic incentives than the best interests of shareholders.
