#3123. Social Security's Trump Bump-Led 2027 COLA Is a Double-Edged Sword for Tens of Millions of Retirees

The projected first silver lining for retirees since 2023 may be offset by worsening solvency issues for America’s top retirement program.

For a majority of retirees, Social Security income is indispensable. A quarter century of annual surveys from national pollster Gallup show that 80% to 90% of retirees consistently rely on their monthly Social Security payout to cover their expenses, in some capacity.

Given how important this program is to the financial well-being of our nation's aging workforce, there's arguably no announcement more anticipated by Social Security's 55 million retired workers than the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) reveal in October.

Social Security's COLA is effectively the "raise" passed on to beneficiaries to offset inflation (rising prices). If Social Security benefits didn't rise in lockstep with inflation, the program's recipients would see their purchasing power dwindle over time.

Social Security's Trump bump is a mixed bag for retirees. Image source: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.

Social Security's 2027 COLA has shaped up as a double-edged sword for tens of millions of retirees. On the one hand, a second consecutive year with a "Trump bump," courtesy of President Donald Trump, should deliver a silver lining for the first time since 2023 for around 29 million retirees. However, this Trump bump also comes with unintended consequences for beneficiaries.

Following the release of the September inflation report on Oct. 14, the Social Security Administration announced that monthly payouts would climb by 3.6% in 2027. This ties for the fifth-largest raise over the last 35 years.

Additionally, it's the sixth straight year in which payouts have risen by at least 2.5%, which is something that hasn't been witnessed since the late 20th century (1988-1997).

While a modest level of inflation is perfectly normal, two of President Trump's policies are primarily responsible for fueling this outsize COLA.

The president's tariff and trade policy has lifted goods price inflation and increased domestic production costs for select items, which are then passed on to consumers. This is the second consecutive year that tariffs have increased the prevailing inflation rate and boosted Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment.

The Trump-led Iran war is also directly influencing consumer prices and, therefore, Social Security payouts. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has led to the largest energy supply disruption in modern history, sending fuel prices soaring.

72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. The 26% increase in benefits over the past 5 years is the biggest 5-year increase since 1982-1986. https://t.co/jMp13XUziC

What makes this 3.6% Trump bump-led Social Security COLA so special is that it may allow approximately 29 million traditional Medicare enrollees to retain more of their benefit in 2027.

Traditional Medicare has three Parts: A (inpatient hospital care), B (outpatient services), and D (prescription drugs). Whereas roughly 99% of workers pay nothing for Part A, Parts B and D have standard monthly premiums. In 2026, the standard monthly premium for Part B is $202.90, and it's typically deducted from a retiree's Social Security benefit.

Since the start of the 21st century, Part B premiums have pretty consistently risen at a quicker pace than Social Security's annual COLA. For example, Social Security raises of 3.2% (2024), 2.5% (2025), and 2.8% (2026) were met by Medicare Part B premium hikes of 5.9% (2024), 5.9% (2025), and 9.7% (2026). When Part B rises substantially faster than Social Security's COLA, it can result in beneficiaries giving up some or all of their annual raise.

According to the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report, the Part B premium is only expected to climb by 3.25% to $209.50 per month in 2027. If this estimate proves accurate, it would mark the first time since 2023 that Social Security's COLA grew faster than the Part B premium, and it would enable tens of millions of retirees to hang onto more of next year's COLA.

While sizable nominal-dollar increases to monthly Social Security checks tend to put smiles on the faces of beneficiaries, outsize raises can come with unintended consequences for America's leading retirement program.

For decades, Social Security's financial foundation has been crumbling. The annually published Social Security Board of Trustees Report has warned of an unfunded long-term (75-year) obligation since 1985.

In other words, the estimated income to be collected in the 75 years after a report is published is expected to be insufficient to cover outlays (benefits plus Social Security's administrative expenses). Ongoing demographic shifts (e.g., rising income inequality, lower net migration into the U.S., and historically low birth rates) have pushed this unfunded obligation through the year 2100 up to an estimated $29.3 trillion.

Yet this gargantuan figure isn't the biggest worry for retirees. Rather, it's the Trustees' projection that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund (OASI) -- the fund that doles out monthly benefits to retired workers and survivors of deceased workers -- will exhaust its asset reserves by the fourth quarter of 2032. These asset reserves are currently invested in special-issue, interest-bearing government bonds, as required by law.

US Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund Assets at End of Year data by YCharts.

The good news is the OASI doesn't need a penny in its asset reserves to continue making payments to eligible beneficiaries. Since the 12.4% payroll tax on earned income generates more than 91% of the income collected by the program, as long as Americans keep working, Social Security can never go bankrupt.

But just because Social Security isn't going bankrupt doesn't mean the program is on solid financial footing. If the OASI's asset reserves are fully depleted, it would confirm that the existing payout schedule, including annual COLAs, isn't sustainable. The Trustees predict that sweeping benefit cuts of 22% will be needed once the OASI's asset reserves run dry.

Social Security's Trump bump-led 2027 COLA may have made things worse. While the Trustees' estimates are based on a laundry list of variables and remain fluid, one core expectation is that Social Security's annual COLA will be modest. That didn't happen in 2027, with Trump's policies leading to the fifth-largest raise since 1993.

A larger-than-normal annual COLA can drain the OASI's already declining asset reserves even faster. This means the projected timeline to benefit cuts may now be less than six years away, and the needed reduction could ultimately be larger than 22%.

Social Security's Trump bump-led COLA is truly a double-edged sword for retirees.

#3119. Archer Aviation Said It Has More Than $6 Billion in Orders. What Does That Actually Mean for Investors?

In 2024, Archer said it had a backlog of more than $6 billion. How has its backlog evolved, and what does it mean for investors?

Archer Aviation (ACHR +14.73%) is angling to become the top player in the fledgling electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) market. As a category of aircraft, eVTOLs could offer big advantages, including requiring smaller launching footprints needed for takeoff, lower noise profiles, less complex engines that require less maintenance, and improved safety.

While the broader eVTOL market has plenty of promise over the long term, that hasn't stopped Archer Aviation stock from struggling over the last year. The company's share price has fallen roughly 62% across the stretch and is now down 70% from its high, pushing the company's market capitalization down to roughly $3.2 billion.

Even though Archer is currently generating very little revenue and its stock has been struggling, the company has made statements that could support a strong bull case. Notably, Archer has said that it already secured more than $6 billion in orders for its Midnight eVTOL aircraft. What does this impressive backlog number mean for investors?

In 2024, Archer said that it had more than $6 billion in orders already lined up for the Midnight eVTOL. The company also said this amounted to roughly 1,200 vehicles on order, meaning each aircraft would be sold for roughly $5 million.

The company has also disclosed that it has substantial contracts lined up with customers, including United Airlines, Japan Airlines and Sumitomo's Soracle joint venture, ITA Airways, and Abu Dhabi Aviation. These are reputable, high-profile customers, and substantial orders from them would seem to represent strong votes of confidence in Archer's tech and the overall commercial viability of its aircraft.

With the company currently valued at roughly $3.2 billion, that means that Archer Aviation is trading at roughly 53% of its previously stated order backlog. Meanwhile, Archer is currently valued at roughly 210 times this year's expected sales.

The company is still seemingly in the very early stages of ramping up its vehicle production, but it has said that it expects to be able to produce roughly 650 Midnight eVTOL aircraft annually by 2030 after scaling up operations to full capacity in the production plant it operates with Stellantis in Georgia.

Based on that timetable, Archer could conceivably fulfill its stated delivery orders by 2030 or 2031 and have generated the accompanying $6 billion in revenue from just the sale of those Midnight crafts. If the company were to achieve that and demonstrate progress toward gross margin targets, its stock would likely skyrocket far above current levels. But there are a couple of huge catches.

Having more than $6 billion in orders for a new type of aircraft that's supposed to disrupt how people travel sounds pretty good on paper. Having big-name airlines as purchasers and a large automotive player like Stellantis as your key manufacturing partner is even better. On the other hand, there's no guarantee that Archer's stated $6 billion order backlog will translate into substantial revenue.

While Archer listed an order backlog of more than $6 billion as a headline number in earnings updates and presentations, it also disclosed in footnotes that this figure was contingent on conditional agreements and the satisfaction of terms in future definitive agreements. In other words, it's not clear that Archer has actually locked in any substantial definitive orders for its Midnight aircraft -- and there's very little of that stated $6 billion backlog that investors can bank on. It gets worse.

Archer Aviation has stated that it has more than $6 billion in orders booked, but it hasn't provided an update on that figure since it published its third-quarter results in November 2024. Even more concerning, the company hasn't mentioned the size of its order book in any subsequent official filings or investor updates.

Archer has not only provided zero updates showing growth in the size of its order book over the last two years; it has also stopped referencing the size of its order book completely. That's not a good sign, and it adds some concerning context to the bigger push into alternative defense industry opportunities that the company has been pursuing through partnerships and acquisitions recently.

#3114. Here's the Yearly Dividend Income $10,000 Provides Across 3 Very Different Yields

Investors need to dig deeper to judge how safe these payouts really are.

Many investors are concerned about the stock market's valuation right now. The extreme level of concentration among a small group of businesses also adds to the fears that a correction is coming. An income-driven strategy might appeal to these investors in today's environment.

There are a lot of dividend stocks out there. While the size of the checks they send shareholders gets the attention, there's always more to the story. Here's the yearly dividend income that $10,000 generates from stocks that offer three very different yields.

The first business on this list is Mastercard (MA -0.49%). It might be the highest-quality company of these three, as indicated by its durable revenue growth and jaw-dropping Q3 operating margin of 59.8%. However, income investors aren't lining up to buy the financial stock. It offers a tiny 0.52% dividend yield. If you buy $10,000 worth of shares, you'd make $52 in yearly income.

It's hard to overlook the growth trajectory, though. In the past decade, Mastercard's dividend went from $0.19 per share quarterly to $0.87, resulting in a huge 358% gain. Given that the business seems to consistently post double-digit diluted earnings-per-share growth every year, investors can bank on the payout continuing to increase in the future.

Consequently, the yield rises over time compared to the cost basis. Let's assume that the dividend is hiked at the same pace in the next decade. If you buy the stock today and wait 10 years, the dividend yield explodes from the current 0.52% to a projected 2.38%. Furthermore, investors will probably benefit from meaningful capital appreciation as well.

Coca-Cola (KO -0.06%) is definitely a better dividend stock than the credit card giant. The leading beverage enterprise pays investors a healthier 2.21% dividend yield. With $10,000 allocated to the stock, you'd capture $221 in annual passive income.

This company is a Dividend King. It has increased its quarterly payout in 64 straight years. That's a mind-boggling streak. The track record clearly shows how successful Coca-Cola has been for such a long period of time, as it has successfully dealt with wars, recessions, bear markets, and a pandemic. Coca-Cola's durability is its most compelling trait.

Investors don't have to worry about the dividend payout coming under threat. This business operates from a position of competitive strength thanks to global customer loyalty and proven pricing power. This is true even in adverse economic times.

And the profits are impressive. Coca-Cola's operating margin was a reported 33.4% during the third fiscal quarter that ended Oct. 2. This supports the company's ability to generate sizable free cash flow, which funds quarterly cash distributions to investors.

The heftiest dividend payer on this list is Ford (F -0.72%), which gives its shareholders a dividend yield of 4.74%. This rivals what the 10-year Treasury currently offers U.S. creditors. On a $10,000 investment, Ford shareholders receive $474 in yearly income.

During the trailing 12 months (ended Sept. 30), Ford's dividend payout ratio was 133%. It paid significantly more than the net income it brought in. Mastercard's payout ratio was 18%, while Coca-Cola's was 62%. This leaves plenty of cushion. On the other hand, from a purely financial perspective, Ford's situation doesn't appear to be sustainable.

The dividend yield is so high because the share price has been on a wildly disappointing run. They have fallen 32% in the past five years (as of Nov. 4). Investors should take this subpar performance as a signal from the market about the quality of this company.

Ford operates with low growth prospects and weak margins. The competitive landscape is fierce. Demand is sensitive to macroeconomic forces. And the business is capital-intensive. Long-term investors will be turned off by these attributes.

#3110. Rocket Lab Just Built a Space Robot

For a price as low as 2x revenue, Rocket Lab has created a new space robots business for itself.

It's been less than six months since space company Rocket Lab (RKLB +15.39%) bought space robotics start-up Motiv Space Systems. The acquisition is already paying off for Rocket Lab.

On Friday, Rocket Lab announced that Motiv -- now known as Rocket Lab Robotics -- will debut its new autonomous robotic arm on a NASA Fly Foundational Robots (FFR) technology demonstration mission in late 2027. Flying aboard a spacecraft in low earth orbit, the robot arm will move across a spacecraft in zero gravity and install a component, demonstrating its ability to manipulate objects and perform repairs and upgrades in space.

A successful demonstration, says Rocket Lab, will open the door to "follow-on missions, from building orbital infrastructure to supporting deep-space exploration." It may also open the gate to a new revenue stream for Rocket Lab.

As tech demonstrations go, this should be an interesting one to watch. What interests me more as an investor is how quickly Rocket Lab may be turning its investment in buying Motiv into new robotics revenue for Rocket Lab.

Why? Rocket Lab paid $40 million in cash up front to acquire Motiv, plus a promise to pay up to $20 million more in stock based on how the acquisition works out -- so up to $60 million total. Even nearly six months after the acquisition, it's still not clear how big a business Motiv is, but estimates range from $3 million to $27 million. But here's the thing:

If Motiv is making even as little as $3 million per year, then Rocket Lab's $60 million purchase price works out to a price-to-sales ratio of 20x on the stock, which is less than half Rocket Lab's own price-to-sales ratio. And if Motiv is generating more than $3 million in revenue (all the way up to $27 million), the price Rocket Lab paid for it becomes correspondingly lower.

Any way you slice it, Rocket Lab got itself a steal of a deal (relative to Rocket Lab's own valuation) when it bought Motiv. And now we know that there's more revenue coming just over the horizon, once Rocket Lab gets Motiv's robotic arm launched on this upcoming NASA mission.

The real reward for Rocket Lab will come, of course, after the tech demonstration proves the robotic arm's use and Rocket Lab starts winning those follow-on missions.

But based on the price it paid for Motiv, even before that race begins, Rocket Lab's already a winner.

#3108. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3105. George Kurtz Just Announced Incredible News for CrowdStrike Investors and the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Industry

Securing artificial intelligence chatbots and agents has become a big challenge for enterprises.

CrowdStrike (CRWD -0.14%) is one of the world's largest cybersecurity vendors. Its Falcon platform is a holistic, all-in-one solution for securing the entire enterprise, from cloud networks to endpoints. The company continues to expand Falcon by introducing new features that will protect customers from the growing threats posed by artificial intelligence (AI).

At CrowdStrike's Fal.Con conference in Europe on Nov. 3, chief executive George Kurtz announced a revolutionary new product called the AI Kill Switch, which allows enterprises to seize full control over the AI agents in their networks.

This product will be a game-changer not only for CrowdStrike, but potentially for the entire AI industry. Here's why.

AI is transforming the threat landscape. Hackers are using the technology to constantly probe corporate networks for vulnerabilities, but businesses are also placing themselves at risk every time they deploy AI chatbots, agents, and other applications.

Agents, for instance, can autonomously perform assigned tasks, but they often require a deep level of access to an organization's sensitive data and digital assets to do so. Hackers are using sophisticated techniques like prompt injection to compromise them, where they disguise their malicious requests as genuine commands to trick agents into handing over sensitive information.

CrowdStrike's Falcon Guardian -- an AI Detection and Response (AIDR) platform -- already offers several tools to combat these threats. It tracks every input and output from trusted agents within the enterprise, which increases the odds of catching malicious behavior. It also inventories every AI application, so it immediately knows if an unauthorized agent is roaming the network.

But the AI Kill Switch is Falcon Guardian's newest weapon, and it's revolutionary. It allows the human security decision maker within the organization to immediately terminate a running agent at its source, cut off its network access, and prevent it from running again. It's the first time enterprises will have full control over their agent fleet, and it's only possible because the Falcon platform is so deeply entrenched in every network and endpoint.

When it comes to deploying powerful technologies, confidence comes from control, so tools like the AI Kill Switch could accelerate enterprise AI adoption.

CrowdStrike had $5.84 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) at the end of its fiscal 2027 second quarter (ended July 31), a 25% increase from the year-ago period. It was the fourth-straight quarter in which ARR growth accelerated.

AI products are driving that incredible momentum. The ARR attributable to AIDR, specifically, almost tripled compared to the first quarter just three months earlier, so there is a mind-boggling amount of demand for Falcon Guardian and its expanding suite of tools.

Before investors race out and buy CrowdStrike stock, they should consider its valuation. It's trading at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 46.6 as I write this on Nov. 4, making it the most expensive name in the cybersecurity industry -- and it's not particularly close. For some perspective, Palo Alto Networks is CrowdStrike's closest competitor, and its P/S ratio is just 23.1.

CrowdStrike is also seven-times as expensive as the Nasdaq-100 index, which has a P/S ratio of 6.3, so it looks heavily overvalued compared to a group of America's highest-quality technology companies. Simply put, investors who are hoping for strong returns in the next 12 months or so might be left disappointed, because CrowdStrike's valuation leaves very little room for upside.

However, CrowdStrike believes it can grow its ARR to $20 billion by fiscal 2036, so investors who are willing to hold its stock for at least the next 10 years can still do well if they buy it today. That forecast might even be conservative considering CrowdStrike predicts its addressable market will be worth $325 billion by calendar year 2030.

Plus, the AI industry is still evolving, so there's no telling how many new opportunities will arise over the next decade.

#3100. In 5 Years, One of These Cryptocurrencies Could Be Worth More Than Bitcoin

If Bitcoin hits one serious snag in particular, a few of its smaller competitors might have a shot at overcoming it.

Today, Bitcoin (BTC -0.19%) has a market cap of $1.6 trillion, making it the biggest cryptocurrency and also one of the biggest assets in the world. That might not be the case within five years: Ethereum (ETH -0.16%), Solana (SOL -0.71%), or Zcash (ZEC -2.54%) could be worth more. But as of Nov. 4, none of those coins were worth even 20% of it.

Closing a market cap gap that large will take some serious problems for Bitcoin and also a few important victories for the contenders. Here is one scenario to consider.

Theoretically, a powerful enough quantum computer could crack Bitcoin's encryption and enable the theft of users' funds. No such computer exists today. However, in March 2026, Google's Quantum AI division estimated that breaking Bitcoin would be substantially easier than previously believed, and it wasn't the first to suggest this.

Crypto experts believe that over 34% of all Bitcoin could be vulnerable to this kind of attack, and the coin's value would take serious punishment if a quantum attack were ever confirmed. That punishment would also hit the institutions holding it through spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

There are a few plans to patch Bitcoin's blockchain to guard against quantum risk, but they're still in draft form and are highly controversial among the Bitcoin developer community. The authors of one such plan, called BIP-361, say that implementing it would take five years, and even starting that process would require a lot of consensus building that is only getting started.

In contrast, Bitcoin's challengers have clearer timelines for mitigating the quantum threat, though none of their plans are finished yet, either.

The Ethereum Foundation is planning to have core quantum protections in place by about 2029. Solana's developers chose a quantum-resistant signature scheme in April 2026, an important precursor to immunizing their blockchain, though they still have no plans to make near-term changes. At the front of the pack are Zcash's developers, who aim to start protecting some transactions from quantum attacks by January 2027.

So the basic conditions for a scenario in which one of those coins surpasses Bitcoin's value in the next five years are that quantum computing continues to become more sophisticated in terms of the available hardware, the available quantum code-breaking algorithms, and the possible attack routes. As a result of either a quantum computing breakthrough or an actual quantum attack on Bitcoin, the market could flee the cryptocurrencies that are thought to be insecure and instead pile into whatever safe havens exist.

Widespread fear of Bitcoin being compromised by a quantum attacker probably wouldn't, in itself, be enough for one of its competitors to surpass it in value. That competitor would also need better economics for holders and a stronger investment thesis, not to mention a decent track record of delivering on its stated objectives.

Zcash is currently in the lead on that front. Its supply policy is largely a copy of Bitcoin's 21-million-coin supply cap, so it can also serve as a scarce store of value. And, starting on Nov. 5, its NU7 upgrade will remove 60% of each block's crypto transaction fees from circulation until about February 2031, when the removed coins will be used to pay miners.

In October, Ethereum shelved a plan to slow the creation of new coins, while Solana's community voted to slow its own coin creation, though that change hasn't taken effect yet.

But neither coin has a supply cap, which means both see their supplies inflate slowly over time. So for either one to have a strong shot at becoming larger than Bitcoin, its ecosystem would need to take off and generate a huge amount of activity, and it would have to implement more supply reforms.

So the most likely outcome is that none of these coins will pass Bitcoin by 2031.

Still, of the contenders, Zcash has the best chance, given its early start on quantum defenses and the similarities that it already shares with Bitcoin.

#3097. Warren Buffett's Top Advice for Investors Bracing for a Market Crash

In addition to portfolio actions, getting ready for a downturn requires mental and emotional preparation.

Warren Buffett's career leading Berkshire Hathaway spans roughly six decades. Over that extended period, he lived through many different environments in which stock prices tanked. While these adverse events certainly tested his temperament, they also gave the Oracle of Omaha invaluable experience. He's better able to navigate the turmoil.

This is the perfect time to turn our attention to the current environment. Despite the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) rising 12% this year (as of Nov. 4), investors are worried that more bad days like Nov. 5 could be coming. Geopolitical turmoil, intense midterm elections, elevated valuations, higher-for-longer interest rates, and concentration in the artificial intelligence trade are sparking fears of a major downturn in the not-too-distant future.

It's time to listen to the legend. If you're bracing for a market crash, consider Warren Buffett's top advice to help in this situation.

No one has a clue when the next bear market will come. But it will happen eventually. According to Hartford Funds, these have occurred approximately every five years since 1945. The best investors are always prepared for the inevitable slide.

If you're expecting a market crash sooner rather than later, building a cash reserve is a smart move. The exact figure can differ. Some investors might be fine with their cash holdings representing 10% of their portfolios, while others might go as high as 30% or more. Either way, this will enable you to play offense and be aggressive when high-quality stocks go on sale.

One of Warren Buffett's most famous quotes suggests that investors should be greedy when everyone else is fearful. Doing the average thing, which is keeping your cool and staying level-headed while the rest of the market is in a state of extreme panic, is what separates good investors from the bad.

Buying the dip is a sound strategy. And having enough cash on hand to act when a bear market hits lays the right foundation. This can support strong portfolio gains over time.

However, there's another side to this coin. Investors shouldn't try to time the market. You might get lucky. But chances are that after you buy stocks, their prices can continue to fall. Predicting the exact tops and bottoms is a waste of effort.

Warren Buffett's successful career was built on patience, discipline, and a relentless focus on the long term. The best course of action for investors who are bracing for a market crash might simply be to continue allocating money to stocks. Decades from now, it won't really matter at what prices you bought.

#3094. Breakfast News: Stocks That Let You Sleep at Night

Motley Fool analysts share four steady stocks to hold through a market slump.

Some mornings, you open your portfolio and wish you hadn’t. The market falls, and your stocks fall with it.

At The Motley Fool, we hold great businesses through every slump. But some stocks make that a lot easier than others. We asked analysts from Team Rule Breakers and Team Hidden Gems to name the ones that do.

Each of these stocks has a history of moving less than the market. A calm chart only tells you so much, though, so our analysts dig into the business strengths behind each pick’s steadiness.

Costco’s (COST -1.13%) big advantage is in its business model. The warehouse giant buys items in such bulk that it can offer customers dirt-cheap prices. This prompts customers to sign up for membership — and keep coming back year after year, as we can see through the company’s 90% membership renewal rate in the U.S. and Canada, its biggest markets.

Meanwhile, Costco can offer customers these bargains because it doesn’t rely on sales of items in its warehouses to drive profit. Instead, the retail giant depends on something you pay before you even begin your shopping trip. I’m talking about membership fees.

In the fiscal year ended Aug. 30, membership fees totaled $5.9 billion on net income of $9.2 billion. Offering membership is high-margin for Costco because it involves little cost, making it a highly profitable part of the business. And the high renewal rates, at these levels over time, offer investors visibility year after year.

Costco could face challenges such as supply chain issues or pressure from rising inflation, but such potential headwinds are temporary and don’t upset the long-term story. Overall, thanks to Costco’s low prices, membership model, lengthy track record of earnings growth, and hefty special dividends paid every few years, this stock is one to hold with confidence through any market environment.

There are a few stocks in my portfolio that I feel are generally “safe” investments, almost certain to preserve my capital over multi-year periods. But my favorite is Realty Income (O -0.77%), a real estate investment trust, or REIT, that owns more than 15,500 net-leased properties in the U.S. and Europe.

The company has a 50+ year history of responsible capital allocation, creating and preserving shareholder value, and raising its dividend over time (116 consecutive quarterly dividend increases).

Realty Income is likely to underperform in periods of rising interest rates, but across multiple economic cycles, it has proven to be a great investment. In fact, since Realty Income went public in 1994, it has averaged a 13.5% annualized total return.

Mastercard (MA -0.49%) is a company I’ve personally owned for almost a decade now and I can honestly say I’ve never lost a wink of sleep over it thanks to itsmassive payments network that spans the globe.

Last quarter, the company saw 9% growth in transactions and 5% growth in cards. This contributed to currency-neutral growth of 12% in net revenue and 19% in adjusted diluted earnings per share from a year ago. Perhaps even more impressive was the company’s 8% increase in worldwide gross dollar volume, thanks in large part to continued growth in cross-border payments.

Mastercard and its competitors remain subject to ongoing global antitrust and legislative scrutiny on routing and interchange fees, which requires consideration. But that’s also been an ongoing narrative for as long as I can remember. Mastercard’s toll booth business model allows it to consistently repurchase shares (share count is down almost 11% over the last five years), and it pays a modest dividend that will continue to grow over time.

Under CEO Michael Miebach and CFO Ling Hai, Mastercard remains well-positioned to capitalize on the global cash-to-digital payment conversion. The company’s phenomenal margins and strong position in the market leave me excited for its future and plenty of good night’s sleep to come.

I think the healthcare giant Johnson & Johnson (JNJ +1.43%) is a perfect example of a stock for preserving capital. It’s a Dividend King that has increased its payout every year for 64 consecutive years, showing incredible resilience through every recession since the 1960s. That’s exactly the consistency I look for in capital preservation.

It’s also one of only two U.S. companies with an AAA credit rating, higher than that of the U.S. government itself. With a dividend yield around 2% and a conservative payout ratio, it generates massive cash to fund future growth.

It’s a sleep-well-at-night stock because people always need medicine and medical devices in any economy. Investors have rewarded that consistency with strong gains over the past year, and J&J has long been a stable compounder across market cycles.

These stocks probably won’t lead the pack when the market is racing ahead. That’s the trade-off. They earn their place when the market falls, because they make it easier to stay invested.

Keep in mind that a steady past doesn’t guarantee a steady future. These stocks can still drop, sometimes sharply. And a portfolio made up only of steady stocks may miss the growth that drives long-term returns. Most investors will want a mix of both.

If the market plunges 30% tomorrow, which stock will you continue to hold with total confidence, and why?

Discuss with friends and family, or become a member to hear what your fellow Fools are saying!

#3091. Lyft: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Lyft's insurance savings are funding rider perks, while its DoorDash bundle is pulling in customers who ride more often.

On its third-quarter earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Lyft (LYFT -4.20%) announced gross bookings, the total dollar value of transactions on its platform, grew 17% year over year to $5.6 billion. The rideshare operator's shift from cash burn to reliable free cash flow gives it the financial flexibility to fund new rider perks and self-driving technology. Three things management said stand out.

Management launched Lyft Go, the company's new rider membership program, integrated with DoorDash's food-delivery subscription. The partnership aims to lower customer acquisition costs while encouraging members to book more rides.

Management reduced the company's cost of revenue by bending the insurance cost curve through safety features and state policy reforms. Lower insurance expenses create financial room for Lyft to offer competitive rider discounts without sacrificing profit margins.

Lyft is preparing for autonomous vehicle (AV), or self-driving car, deployments by managing fleet facilities and matching passenger demand in select cities. Management focuses on deep technical integrations with key technology partners rather than spreading resources across dozens of developers.

Rideshare demand is expanding across North America, and management is eager to capitalize on record driver hours and faster pickup times. Lyft relies on customer retention programs, international expansion, and operational efficiency to drive future earnings, while monitoring pricing discipline.

Management maintains capital discipline by funding growth with balance-sheet cash flow while repurchasing shares. Operational rigor in core ridesharing provides the capital needed for long-term mobility investments.

#3089. Chewy vs. Target: Which Retailer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Chewy's subscription loyalty and Target's store-based reach are very different bets, and their valuation gap stands out.

Determining whether to invest in Chewy Inc. (CHWY -1.91%) or Target Corp. (TGT +0.29%) requires weighing the rapid growth of digital-first specialty retail against the established stability of a massive, multi-category brick-and-mortar powerhouse.

Chewy focuses exclusively on the pet category, using its subscription-heavy model to build deep customer loyalty. Target operates as a broad-line retailer, offering everything from groceries to apparel. While both compete for consumer dollars, they offer different profiles for investors looking to balance growth potential with established stability.

In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, Chewy noted it sells pet products, supplies, and prescriptions through its websites and mobile applications. It relies heavily on its Autoship subscription service, which provides recurring revenue and convenience for over 21 million active customers. The company also operates the largest pet pharmacy in America and is expanding into veterinary clinics.

In FY 2025, revenue reached about $12.6 billion, representing a growth of roughly 6.2% year over year. The company reported a net income of approximately $222.8 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin of around 1.8%, which measures the percentage of revenue remaining after all expenses.

As of its February 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 1.0x, meaning its total debt equals its shareholder equity. Its current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term debts, is roughly 0.9x. Free cash flow reached about $562.4 million, though note that stock-based compensation (or, SBC) represented roughly 43% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Target provides a curated multi-category assortment of general merchandise and grocery products within the competitive environment for retail stocks. It enhances its selection through strategic partnerships with major brands like Apple Inc. (AAPL -0.52%), Starbucks Corp. (SBUX -0.71%), and Ulta Beauty Inc. (ULTA -0.78%). The company also utilizes its physical stores as local fulfillment hubs for digital sales and operates a successful loyalty program.

In FY 2025, revenue reached around $104.8 billion, which was a decrease of approximately 1.7% compared to the prior year. Despite the slight dip in sales, the company achieved a net income of roughly $3.7 billion. This performance resulted in a net margin of about 3.5% for the fiscal period.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, Target carries a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 1.3x. Its current ratio is roughly 0.9x, indicating its short-term assets are slightly lower than its short-term liabilities. The company generated free cash flow of nearly $2.8 billion, providing ample capital for its dividends and internal growth initiatives.

Chewy faces intense competition from online retailers like Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN -0.35%) and various mass merchandisers. It relies heavily on third-party shipping logistics and cloud infrastructure, making it vulnerable to service disruptions. Operational risks also include potential supply chain issues, particularly regarding private brand sourcing from international markets.

Target faces competitive risks from other retailers and digital platforms regarding pricing, fulfillment, and technological integration. It is susceptible to reputational damage, inventory shrinkage due to theft, and disruptions in its complex global supply chain. The company also manages ongoing legal and regulatory risks, including potential worker classification challenges at its Shipt subsidiary.

Target appears significantly more affordable based on its Forward P/E, which uses future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio measures market capitalization relative to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Well-known retailer Target is in the first year of its multi-year turnaround strategy, which aims to restore top-line growth and margins. The effort has been going well, but there is concern that elevated gas prices, which raise transportation costs and reduce consumers' spending capabilities, could derail the turnaround story over the near term. But to its benefit, Target is the most-followed retailer on social media platforms, has a strong women's clothing business, and should be able to capture more food business by expanding the section in remodeled stores. About half of Target sales include food items of some sort.

For fiscal 2027, Target is expected to see a sales gain of nearly 6%, to more than $110 billion, which is pretty good considering the pinched American consumer. Net income should improve much more strongly, to more than $1 billion, up to $4.7 billion.

Meanwhile, Chewy is establishing a steady growth pattern. In a recently reported quarter, management noted that its Autoship program grew faster than overall sales, implying that many customers' standing orders will continue to provide a solid base for the company. The company also believes that in the long run, veterinarian and general pet health services are a huge untapped market for Chewy. The business recently closed on the acquisition of Modern Animal, which delivers high profitability per location and is a strong complement to Chewy's existing business.

For fiscal 2027, sales are seen rising 7% to $13.5 billion, with net income up more than 40% to around $317 million, according to consensus analyst estimates. American consumers have shown they will spend up to take care of their pets.

However, Chewy likely doesn't have a great competitive moat against brick-and-mortar competitors like PetSmart and Petco Health and Wellness Co Inc. (WOOF -0.67%).

Here, the choice is between two retailers that execute well, though with different profiles on how they make their money. There are times when a retail stock should command a premium, but in this case, the better approach is to go for good value in the shares. Target and Chewy have the same P/S ratio. But Target is much more affordable on a P/E basis, right around the average forward P/E for S&P 500 stocks.

Brendan Coffey has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon, Apple, Chewy, Starbucks, Target, and Ulta Beauty. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3085. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#3083. Celtics brutalize injury-riddled Hornets 119-80 for 2nd NBA Cup win

Jayson Tatum came back from a rest game with a head of steam, and the Charlotte Hornets stood no chance with five notable injuries.

Tatum's 34 points (24 of which he scored in the first half) led the Boston Celtics to a 119-80 win over the Hornets in the teams' first matchup of the season and Boston's first stop in a 4-game road trip. The win gives the C's a 7-2 record on the season and an NBA Cup group play record of 2-0 in East Group C.

Boston now leads the group by record, and sports a +53 scoring differential, which leads the group by 44 points. The winner of each group, plus two wild cards from each conference, will make it to the NBA Cup's knockout rounds.

The Celtics starting squad tonight included Derrick White, Jordan Walsh, Paul George, Jayson Tatum, and Neemias Queta. Boston's injury report was clear.

The Hornets started Coby White, Brandon Miller, Grayson Allen, Naz Reid, and Ryan Kalkbrenner. Kon Knueppel, Moussa Diabate, and former Celtics Grant Williams and Dennis Schroder, sat out with injuries. Miller also left the game at the half with right groin soreness.

Tatum started hot with an easy three-pointer off a screen, as the Hornets opened up the game with Reid guarding him. But he did not spam that matchup off the bat. Instead, the opening minutes were defined by energy and activity. George hit a three-pointer after Queta rebounded a midrange clunker. George and Queta both stuffed a couple Hornets shot attempts. White got a defensive rebound, ran the length of the floor and hit a transition 3 to give the C's a 9-2 lead three minutes into the game.

White and JT kept the momentum going for a few more minutes. White scored on back-to-back and-1s, including a 4-point play, to get 7 points in 15 seconds of game time. Tatum scored the next two buckets and put Boston up 21-7 with less than 7 minutes to go. At that point, the C's had connected on 5-7 three-point attempts.

However, the offense started dragging after that as the Hornets seemed to settle in. Payton Pritchard hit a sweet step-back three-pointer, and the Celtics' activity didn't slow, but shots stopped falling so effortlessly. In response, Coach Joe Mazzulla called a timeout and subbed in Baylor Scheierman and Sam Hauser to inject some offense. Scheierman immediately made an impact by splashing a three-pointer, then drew a foul on the Hornets to get the ball back for the C's soon after.

Luckily for the Celtics, Tatum stayed hot. He drove to the basket for a couple nice layups, got to the line and hit a pair of free throws, got an and-1 with another layup, then nailed a three-pointer. That wasn't the end of it, though. Before the quarter ended, he assisted on a deep (and I mean DEEP) Hauser three-pointer, and got the ball to Scheierman for an attempt from behind the arc at the buzzer. Scheierman missed the shot, but it was a quality look.

By the end of the opening frame, Tatum already had 18 points and Boston led Charlotte 40-20.

The C's stayed active in the second quarter despite the big lead. Mitchell Robinson opened the frame with a tough finish through contact inside (of course, he missed his free throw) and was all over the boards. Without Tatum, who regularly takes a rest at the start of second quarters, the team struggled to make its shots — but so did the Hornets. Both teams scored a combined 3 points over the first 3 minutes of the second quarter.

Boston began to break out of that lull around the 8-minute mark of the second frame, when White hit a three-pointer. That shot seemed to take the lid off the basket for the C's, as George cashed in on a floater soon after. George then hit a three-pointer, which Luka Garza followed up on the next possession with another 3. Almost halfway through the quarter, the Celtics led 53-25.

JT came back into the game with 5:34 left to go in the second frame, and after about a minute, hit a beautiful step-back 3 to keep the offense rolling. It was the first of three straight offensive possessions with made 3s for the Celtics, as Pritchard and Tatum hit on the team's next 2 three-point attempts. Those buckets helped secure Boston's first 30-point lead of the game, as the C's led 62-31 with 3 minutes left to go in the half.

Naz Reid hit back-to-back shots to cut into the lead, but White hit a couple of his own, and Robinson got a block that led to an open Hauser 3, leaving the Celtics with an imposing 70-39 lead at the half. Boston won the quarter 30-19.

Jayson Tatum, who was red-hot in the first half, racked up 24 points on 57.1% shooting from the field and 5-8 shooting from three-point range. He also had 4 rebounds and 6 assists before the break.

Boston's second-leading scorer was Derrick White, who had 18 points, 4 rebounds, 5 assists, and a steal at the half. No other Celtic had more than 8 points, but the team as a whole shot 54.8% from three-point range.

On the other end of the court, Naz Reid led Charlotte in scoring at the half with 10 points. The Hornets shot only 28.3% from the field and 21.7% from three-point range in the first half.

The Celtics maintained their energetic defense from the first half, but the offense briefly stuttered to open the second. Nevertheless, Queta got the scoring going with a couple nice buckets, including a hook shot and an impressive one-handed alley-oop on a pass from JT. Tatum continued to make his mark on the game by hitting a couple free throws, then assisting on a tough Walsh dunk and-1. Four minutes into the third quarter, the C's had a 79-45 lead.

The Celtics didn't let themselves become complacent with such a lead. Tatum, Pritchard, and Scheierman kept the offense churning, while the defense stayed active and refused to allow Charlotte's offense to get in a flow. JT was unstoppable driving to the rim and reached 30 points on a layup with 4:26 remaining in the third. Robinson threw down a couple hefty alley-oops, the second of which put the game out of reach entirely, as the C's had a 94-53 lead with less than 2 minutes to go in the frame.

By the end of the third quarter, which the Celtics won 26-18, Boston led by 39 points.

The C's opened the fourth with Pritchard, Hauser, Hugo Gonzalez, Mike Conley, and Luka Garza on the floor. While the Hornets scored the first 4 points of the quarter, Hauser and Pritchard splashed a couple three-pointers that inspired Charlotte to call a timeout, raise the white flag, and send in its reserves. Boston subbed in Ron Harper Jr. for Pritchard, but otherwise kept the same squad on the court to run up the lead.

Without Pritchard, Gonzalez and RHJ led the Celtics offense. After Gonzalez hit a 3 with 5:35 to go in the final frame, the Celtics had a 112-67 lead. It was such an insurmountable lead that NBA.com's NBA Cup standings page showed Boston's group play record as 2-0 about halfway through the fourth quarter.

The C's offense was a little clunky the rest of the way, but a couple three-pointers from Walsh and Garza inflated the lead to 118-74 with about 2 minutes left in the game.

Tatum finished the game with 34 points on 56.3% shooting from the field and 11-11 free throws, 7 rebounds, 9 assists, and a steal.

White failed to score a single point in the second half, but still finished as Boston's second-leading scorer for the night, with 18 points. The only other Celtic to finish in double digits was Pritchard, who had 12 points.

The team as a whole shot 45.8% from the field and 54.5% from three-point range. Boston's 24 made three-pointers is a new NBA Cup record.

Reid led the Hornets with 14 points, while Sion James had 11 points off the bench. Overall, Charlotte shot 29.3% from the floor and 22% from behind the arc.

Boston's next game will be against the Milwaukee Bucks at 8 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 8, at the Fiserv Forum in Milwaukee. The road trip will then take the C's to Philadelphia and Toronto.

The C's next NBA Cup group play game won't be until Tuesday, Nov. 24, when they will face the Wizards. It will be the Celtics' third of four group play matches before knockout rounds begin on Friday, Dec. 4.

#3076. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

Heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

"CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable company, regardless of market conditions.

Richardson ranks No. 478 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Crescent Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 2:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

#3062. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#3052. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."
